units.la: {R}EM publico nec ingratam nec inutilem nos facturos, visum est, si hasce de operationibus Dæmonum dissertationes secunda vice in publicum edi accuraremus. Fervet hoc tempore, occasione libri cujusdam belgice à viro docto conscripti, hæc quæstio. Eo de libro arbitrari nostri judicii res haut est. Has tantum tecum communicamus dissertationes, idque duplici potissimum nomine, cum ut eædem fili sint tibi loco, quo errabunda vestigia regas, quodque in ipsa adyta hujus litis te ducat, tum maxime ut constet, quam longe Philosophiæ Cartefianæ Σλοιχεῖα remota sint à fundamentis, quibus suum ædificium libri Belgici autor superstruit, & quam iniqui rerum arbitri sint ii, qui in triviis, in compitis, & ubi non, imperito vulgo persuadere sumsummo nituntur opere, Scriptoris Belgici sententiam exPhilosophia Cartesiana pullulare, quum ejus philosophiae femina plane in contrarium ducant, ac <bl>δὶς διὰ παθῶν</bl> ab illa differant. Autor harum exercitationum est D. Tobias Andreae, Medicinae & Philosophiae Doctor, utriusque facultatis primum Tuiscoburgi ad Rhenum, exinde Francofurti ad Viadrum, tum in illustri Gymnasio Sylvaducensi, denique Franequerae, ubi & diem suum obiit, Prosessor Celeberrimus, a quo plura subacti ingenii, & judicii acerrimi, quo valebat, haberes monimenta, si longioris vitae usura ipsi frui, datum fuisset. Adjecimus nonnulla his affinia, ex scriptis Wittichii, qui sparsit, & nomen toto sparget in orbe suum, tralatitie excerpta. Quibus plura addi possent, nisi hæc sufficere persuasi essemus. Vale & his fruere nobiscum.
units.tr: Since we judged that these dissertations on the operations of demons would be neither unwelcome nor useless to the public, we saw fit to take care that they be published a second time. At present this question is hotly debated, prompted by a book on the subject written in Dutch by a learned man. We do not presume to pass judgement on that book. We share with you only these dissertations, for two main reasons: first, so that they may serve you as a thread to guide your wandering steps and lead you into the very sanctuary of this dispute; and second, and above all, so that it may be clear how far the elements [Σλοιχεῖα] of Cartesian philosophy are removed from the foundations on which the author of the Dutch book builds his edifice, and how unfair those judges of the matter are who, at crossroads and street corners, strive with the utmost effort to persuade the untutored crowd that the opinion of the Dutch writer springs from Cartesian philosophy, when the teachings of that philosophy lead in the opposite direction and differ from it twice over through the passions [δὶς διὰ παθῶν]. The author of these exercises is Mr. Tobias Andreae, Doctor of Medicine and of Philosophy, first professor in both faculties at Tuiscoburg on the Rhine, then at Frankfurt on the Oder, then at the illustrious Gymnasium at Sylvaducum, and finally at Franeker, where he also died. He was a most celebrated professor, and you would have had from him more memorials of his vigorous talent and most keen judgement, had he been granted the enjoyment of a longer life. We have added some things akin to these, excerpted in the customary way from the writings of Wittich, who has spread his name, and will spread it throughout the world. More could be added, but we were persuaded that these would suffice. Farewell, and enjoy these with us.

units.la: ARDUUM satis esse, non historicè, sed methodo veré Philosophica, de vi & potentia Angelorum in corpora tractare, per quàm notum est illi, qui vastum Philosophiæ Oceanum longiùs ingressi sunt; norunt enim, quòd demum hoc trajecto de hac materia pro dignitate agi possit. Quapropter, ne quis putet, me scribendi cacoethe aut ingenij quodam pruritu ad tam sublimem materiam publicè ventilandam abreptum esse, permitte, Lector Benevole, in limine te ut paucis morer, quo rationem, quæ me ad hoc exercitium invita vit, cognoscas. Annus jam vertitur septimus, quo in Belgio hærens, inter amicos quosdam quæstionem hanc ventilari andiverim, an solo Naturæ lumine probari possit Angelos, ceu bonos, ceu malos, dari. Postquam de ea pro & contra diu disputatum fuit, & res in suspen-
units.tr: It is indeed a difficult task to treat of the power and might of angels over bodies by a truly philosophical method, not a historical one, as is known to those who have gone further into the vast ocean of Philosophy; for they know that only after this crossing can the matter be handled as it deserves. Therefore, lest anyone think that I was carried away into publicly airing so lofty a subject by a desire for writing or some itch of wit, permit me, kind Reader, to detain you briefly at the threshold, so that you may learn the reason that invited me to this exercise. It is now seven years since, while staying in Belgium, I heard among some friends this question debated: whether it can be proved by the light of Nature alone that angels exist, both good and evil. After it had been disputed for a long time, for and against, and the matter had been left in suspen-

units.la: sa fo quasi relicta, seriùs cogitare de ea incepi, & quia solito tum ociosior eram, hac occasione excitatus, illam quastionem accuratiùs examinare coepi: Et quidem eousque me eam penetrâsse mihi videbar, quòd quidem facile mihi esset à priore demonstrare, eorum possibilitatem, seu quod non repugnet Angelos dari, at mon, nisi à posteriore, & quidem illis saltem, qui non pertinaciter omnem omnibus historiis fidem derogant, quòd sint: Imò ad rem perveniens experiebar, nec hoc modo posse satis dilucidè probari, Angelos bonos dari, at solùm malos. Rudes igitur quos de hac materia habui conceptus, ita uti sub manu nascebantur, in chartam raptim conjicere incepi, at à continuatione ipsorum, tædium, quod oritur ex contemplatione obiecti illius odiosissimi, quod Mens nostra non distincte, nisi cum horrore considerare potest (quapropter voluntas se statim ab illo se jungit, hoc est, odio habet, & ab ejus contemplatione citò recerecedit) removit, ut ad finem omnia quæ tractanda proposueram non deduxerim. Imò nunquam animum inducere potui, ut ad incudem & exactiorem limam priores conceptus revocarem, multò minus ut publicâ luce donarem: Præsertim cum prater hoc considerarem, quòd, etsi accurate satis priores conceptus examinâssem, paucissimi tamen futuri essent, qui de eis æquum judicium ferrent, quia cognitionem totius Philosophiæ & Medicinæ non superficiariam præsupponunt. Quod quidem primo intuitu mirum videri multis videbitur, cùm putent experientiâ satis constare, quam vim & potentiam Angeli in corpora habent; At cùm eo perventum erit, ut non quæratur amplius an habeant, sed quomodo explicent, postulatum hoc iniquum esse non dicent; Et continuâs em firmiter in eodem proposito, nec vel minimam partem horum examini novo subjecissem, & publici juris fecissem, nisi me instantes petitiones GENEROSI & PRÆ-
units.tr: sion, as if left aside, I began to think about it more seriously, and since I was then more idle than usual, roused by this occasion, I began to examine that question more carefully. And indeed I seemed to myself to have penetrated it so far that I could easily demonstrate from the former (a priori) their possibility, that is, that it is not contradictory for angels to exist; but not from the latter (a posteriori), and that only for those at least who do not stubbornly deny all faith to all histories, that they do exist. Indeed, on coming to the matter itself I found that in this way it could not be sufficiently clearly proved that good angels exist, but only evil ones. So I began to jot down hastily on paper the crude notions I had on this matter, just as they arose under my hand; but in continuing them, a weariness arose from contemplating that most hateful object, which our mind can consider distinctly only with horror (so the will at once turns away from it, that is, hates it, and quickly withdraws from its contemplation). This removed me, so that I did not carry out to the end everything I had proposed to treat. Indeed I could never bring myself to recall the earlier conceptions to the anvil and a more exact file, much less to give them to the light of publication, especially since I considered besides that, although I had examined the earlier conceptions accurately enough, very few would be there who would pass a fair judgment on them, since they presuppose a knowledge of the whole of Philosophy and Medicine, and not a superficial one. This will at first sight seem strange to many, who think that experience sufficiently establishes what power and might the angel has over bodies; but when it has come to the point that one no longer asks whether they have it, but how they exercise it, they will not say that this demand is unfair. units.la: Cùm enim curiosissimus sit in observationibus rarioribus, quæ in Maximo Naturæ Theatro fiunt, contemplandis & inquirendis, atque hoc tempore in vicino Comitatu Meursensi mirabile se exemplum exhibuerit Genii cujusdam cum hominibus loquentis, variaque mira facientis, quæ omnes stupent; Interimque laudatus DOMINUS ex tractatu de Passionibus Animæ, (quem Philosophorum Princeps RENAT. CARTESIVS literato orbi reliquit, cujusque explicationem in privato Collegio circa idem tempus suscepi.) satis animadverteret, posse juxta illa, quae deconjunctione mentis nostra cum corpore nostro demonstravi, multa quoque de conjunctione mentium aliarum, & ita mali Genii, cum corporibus diversis, summe probabilia dici, petiit, ut, quos apud me in schedis dispersos viderat, de hac materia conceptus meos reassumerem, & saltem aliquos eorum in ordinem redigerem. Amicae, igitur petitioni locum concedens, constitui Exercitatione una aut altera publica experiri, quid in novo hoc studii genere valeam, ut placido doctorum examini conceptus meos subjiciens vel occasionem habeam eos ulterius perpoliendi & latius deducendi, aut immutandi, vel corrigendi; vel in eo statu in quo sunt relinquendi; vel saltem excellentia ingenia incitandi, ut curiosius hanc materiam pertractent. Hoc enim praecipue fine eos publici juris facio. Ut autem melius hoc fiat, quamvis integram Philosophiam praesupponi debere innuerim, tamen quaedam generaliora de Mente & corpore præmittenda erunt, ut ex iis particulariora commodius explicentur. Et de Mente quidem nostra præcipuè, quia de illa non ita quilibet cogitat, at de corporibus, se plus quàm de mentibus cognoscere, quilibet sibi præsumit. Hæc igitur sequentia sunto.
units.tr: For he, being most curious in contemplating and investigating the rarer observations that occur in the greatest Theatre of Nature, and having lately shown a remarkable example in the neighbouring County of Meurs of a certain spirit that speaks with men and performs various wonders, at which everyone marvels; and the aforesaid Lord, from the treatise on the Passions of the Soul, which the Prince of Philosophers RENÉ DESCARTES left to the literate world, and whose explanation I undertook in a private college about the same time, sufficiently observed that, according to those things which I demonstrated concerning the conjunction of our mind with our body, many things could also be said, with great probability, concerning the conjunction of other minds, and so of evil spirits, with various bodies. He asked that I take up again my thoughts on this matter, which he had seen scattered among my papers, and reduce at least some of them to order. Yielding to his friendly request, I resolved to test in one or two public exercises what I am worth in this new kind of study, so that by submitting my thoughts to the calm examination of learned men I might have an opportunity either to polish them further and develop them more widely, or to change or correct them, or to leave them in the state in which they are, or at least to stir excellent minds to treat this matter more carefully. For I publish them chiefly with this aim. But so that this may be done better, although I have hinted that a whole philosophy must be presupposed, nevertheless some more general matters concerning Mind and body must be set out first, so that the more particular things may be explained more conveniently from them. And concerning our Mind especially, because on that subject not everyone thinks in the same way, whereas about bodies everyone presumes that he knows more than about minds. Let these things therefore follow.

units.la: CAPUT I. De Mentium Finitarum Potentia, quam in CORPORA exercent in genere.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. On the power of finite minds over bodies in general.

units.la: QUI naturam Mentis corporisque distinctè ex prima Philosophia cognovit, non inficias ibit, quòd nec de mentis essentia fit, corporicuidam, nec de corporis essentia, ut cuidam Menti jungatur, quippe utriusque essentia toto, quod ajunt, cælo differt. Quòd si igitur Mens quædam corpori conjungi debet, perinde est an magno vel parvo, subtili, crasso, fluido, molli, raro, duro; quadrato, rotundo, noto, quiescenti; imò multis corporibus ribus simul, aut uni; & sic porro, jungatur. Et viceversâ, si corpus Menti cuidam jungendum sit, aeque cum mala, quàm bona; perfectiori quàm imperfectâ; innumeris quàm unâ, conjungi potest.
units.tr: Whoever has known the nature of mind and of body distinctly from first philosophy will not deny that a mind does not come to be the essence of some body, nor the essence of a body come to be joined to some mind. The essence of each differs from the other as far as, so to speak, heaven differs from earth. If, then, some mind must be joined to a body, it makes no difference whether the body is large or small, subtle or thick, fluid or soft, rare or hard, square or round, at rest or in motion; indeed, whether it is joined to many bodies at once or to one, and so on. And conversely, if a body must be joined to some mind, it can be joined equally to a bad mind as to a good one, to a more perfect mind rather than an imperfect one, to countless minds rather than to one.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Conjunctionem autem hanc nullo modo fieri per ullum contactum: quo veluti magnes & ferrum sibi invicem adhærent; aut se succina pulcra maritant; aut etiam spiritus, omnes per artus & membra corporis diffusus, eique mixtus est, quatenus omnes eorum poros permeat; aut ullo alio modo conjunctionis corporeæ conceptibili, quo corpora ex duobus fiunt unum, hoc itidem ex naturâ Mentis perceptâ æque constare suppono. Quippe mens nec superficiem habet, juxta quam illè contactus fieri deberet. Sed illa conjunctio unicè consistit in operatione, quam aut hæ duæ substantiæ diversæ in se invicem mutuò habere possunt, aut solum mens in corpus illud, cui se jungit; uti nec implicat corpus quoddam solum in Mentem cui junctum est, agere posse. Atque in hoc unicè præsentia Mentium, aut esse hîc vel ibi, consistit.
units.tr: Moreover, I take it that, from the nature of mind as we perceive it, this conjunction is in no way brought about by any contact, such as that by which a magnet and iron cling to each other, or fine pieces of amber unite with one another, or a spirit diffused through all the joints and members of the body and mixed with it, insofar as it penetrates all its pores, or by any other conceivable mode of corporeal conjunction by which two bodies become one. For a mind has no surface along which such a contact could take place. Rather, that conjunction consists solely in the operation which these two diverse substances can have mutually on each other, or in the operation of the mind alone upon the body to which it is joined; just as it is not conceivable that a body alone can act upon a mind to which it is joined. In this alone consists the presence of minds, or their being here or there.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Non minus, ut probatum assumo. quòd nulla Mens finita fe pro suo arbitrio alicui corpori, multò minus cuivis jungere possit, sed hanc conjunctionem aut immediate à Deo fieri, aut saltem ex Dei jussu, aut etiam ipsius conniven-tia.
units.tr: I assume, as is proved, that no finite mind can join itself at its own pleasure to any body, much less to any body whatever; but this conjunction is brought about either immediately by God, or at least by God's command, or else with his connivance.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Sic Mentem nostram corpori suo ab ipso Deo junctam esse, receptissima est sententia, in qua & nos acquiescimus. Ad minimum illam se corpori suo non pro suo arbitrio junxisse, ex illo liquere videtur, quòd aliàs etiam posset quotiefcunque liberet ab eo se sejungere; iterumque ei se conjungere per ejusdem liberi arbitrii potestatem, quâ se primo ei conjunxit, cujus tamen contrarium conscientia quemlibet docet.
units.tr: That our mind is joined to its body by God himself is the most widely received opinion, and we too assent to it. At least, it appears from this that our mind did not join itself to its body at its own pleasure: otherwise it could also separate itself from that body whenever it wished, and again join itself to it by the same power of free will by which it first joined itself to it. Yet conscience teaches everyone the contrary.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Cùm igitur Mens nostra se indifferenter ad corpus, omnesque eius assectiones (juxta thef. 1.) habeat, & ab ipso Deo immediatè corpori suo (juxta thef. seq.) jungatur, non potest non attendenti constare, quòd etiam ipsi perinde sit, quibus modis illi per corpus hoc vel illud quid significatur, sic ut omnes motus corporei, quibus assicitur, signa ipsi sint corporum extra illam consistentium, illamque afficientium, non formalia (uti in scholis loquuntur ) sed tantùm materialia, hoc est, nullo modo cum ipsis rebus convenientia, sed solùm ipsi occasionem, ut jam hæc, jam illa percipiat, præbentia; ac præcisé quidem illa solùm, quæ voluit significari per illa hic, qui hoc mentis corporisque conjugium pro suo arbitrio constituit, & inviolabileesse voluit, scilicet ipse Deus. Non aliter uti campanarum sonus, aut vexillorum varietas nullam convenientiam habens cum rebus, quas significat, id solùm quod magistratus voluit per illa indicari, significat, aut sicuti vocabula fere omnia, quibus utimur ad conceptus nostros exprimendos, talia signa sunt, illud significantia, quod vulgò aut cuicunque illorum inventori placuit illis significare: ut v. gr. vox Deus seu scripta seu prolata, & infinitum illud Ens, quod per eam repræsentatur, nullo modo conveniunt.
units.tr: Since, then, our mind stands indifferently towards the body and all its affections (as in thesis 1), and is joined immediately by God himself to its body (as in the following thesis), it cannot but be evident to anyone who attends to it that it is equally indifferent by what means this or that is signified to it through this or that body. Thus all the bodily motions by which it is affected are signs to it of bodies existing outside it and affecting it, but signs that are not formal (as they say in the schools) but only material; that is, they are in no way similar to the things themselves, but merely give the mind an occasion to perceive now this, now that. And they signify precisely those things which he who established this marriage of mind and body at his own pleasure, and willed it to be inviolable, namely God himself, chose to be signified by them. It is no different from the sound of bells or the variety of flags, which, having no resemblance to the things they signify, signify only what the magistrate wished to be indicated by them; or as nearly all the words we use to express our concepts are such signs, signifying that which the common people, or whoever invented them, chose them to signify. For example, the word God, whether written or spoken, and that infinite Being which is represented by it, have no resemblance to one another at all.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Et hoc manifestissimé etiam nobis conscientia dictat, quâ certi sumus, quòd ver. gr. ille motus, qui nobis præsentat lumen, hoc est, cujus occasione Mens nostra excitatur, ut percipiat seu cogitet de corpore lucido, tam necessariò illud repræsentet, ut non possimus pro nostro beneplacito eam per-ceceptionem immutare, sic ut ejus loco v. gr. sonum, aut musicam, aut simile quid, percipiamus Idemque de omnibus omnino perceptionum speciebus, quæ fiunt mediante corpore, verissimum est.
units.tr: Conscience also dictates this most manifestly to us, since we are certain that, for example, that motion which presents to us light (that is, the motion on whose occasion our mind is stirred to perceive or think of a luminous body) represents it so necessarily that we cannot, at our own pleasure, change that perception so that in its place we perceive, for example, a sound, or music, or something similar. And the same is entirely true of all kinds of perceptions which come about through the body.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Imò, quod majus est, tam arctam & immediatam hanc Mentis nostræ cum suo corpore Deus voluit esse copulam, ut quamdiu corpus quoad omnia bene dispositum est, nec Mens per profundiffimas meditationes fe quasi corpori suo subducit, non possit non omnes illos motus corporis, qui sunt fatis potentes ad nervos nostros validé agitandos, percipere, uti id eâdem conscientiâ nobis constat. Nam ita non solùm perceptionem luminis mutare non poteft (uti dicûum) sed nec illud non percipere cùm oculos intrat, quamdiu organa visûs fe bene habent, & Mens à corpore suo alienata non est. Ex quibus consequitur quòd toties eadem perceptio in Mente nostra necessariò existat, quoties idem plane motus ipsi offertur.
units.tr: Indeed, and what is greater, God willed this bond between our mind and its body to be so close and immediate that, as long as the body is well disposed in all respects, and the mind is not withdrawn from its body as if by most profound meditations, it cannot fail to perceive all those movements of the body which are powerful enough to stir our nerves strongly, as our own consciousness assures us. For in this way the mind not only cannot change the perception of light (as was said), but also cannot fail to perceive it when it enters the eyes, as long as the organs of sight are in good condition and the mind is not estranged from its body. From these things it follows that the same perception necessarily arises in our mind whenever the very same movement is presented to it.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Loquor solùm de motibus corporis, quia (ut alias rationes taceam) facilé probare possem, quòd Mens nostra stra non à toto suo corpore immediatè afficiatur, sed ab ipso solùm, quod in illo fluidum & agitatum est, ac ob id ad varia menti repræsentanda aptum, & quale præcisè solùm judico esse spiritum animalem in ventriculis cerebri præsertim confluentem, qui nuncius quasi est illorum omnium, quæ menti de suo aliisquè corporibus indicari debent, & instrumentum vicevería, quo mens primò, vel immediatè & principaliter utitur, si quid in corpore ef-ficere velit. Sed quia hoc nimis longum foret, ea quæ huc spectant, tanquam certa & ingeniosè explicata, ex tractatu incomparabilis Philosophi Renati Cartesii, de passionibus animæ, & præsertim §. 13. 14. seqq. assumi-nus.
units.tr: I speak only of the motions of the body, because (to pass over other reasons) I could easily show that our mind is not immediately affected by its whole body, but only by that part of it which is fluid and agitated, and therefore fit to represent various things to the mind. I judge that this is precisely the animal spirit, especially as it gathers in the ventricles of the brain. It is, as it were, the messenger of all those things which must be indicated to the mind concerning its own body and other bodies, and conversely the instrument which the mind first and immediately and principally uses if it wishes to effect anything in the body. But since this would be too long, we assume those matters that pertain here as certain and cleverly explained, from the treatise of the incomparable philosopher René Descartes, On the Passions of the Soul, and especially §§ 13, 14 and following.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Nobis ad institutum nostrum assequéndum sufficiat in genere advertisse, primò, quòd pro omni diversitate motûs Spirituum animalium à diversâ eo-rum magnitudine, figurâ, soliditate &c. tum nervorum multivaria positione &c. pendente, infinitè diversa repræsentamina, non autem immediatè ab organis ipsis imo ne quidem ab ipsis fibrillis nervorum, menti sistuntur; uti insomnia dormientium & vigilantium memoria quoque & vis imaginandi satis probant:
units.tr: For our purpose it is enough to have noted in general, first, that for every variation in the motion of the animal spirits, which depends on their different magnitude, shape, solidity and so on, and on the many possible positions of the nerves, infinitely varied representations are presented to the mind. These are not presented immediately by the organs themselves, nor even by the fibrils of the nerves, as the dreams of sleepers and the memory and power of imagination of the waking sufficiently prove.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Secundo, quod motus spirituum animalium nullo modo à mente, in quantum simpliciter motus, pendeat, seu ab ipsa producatur; non solum, tum quando menti per eas quid repræsentatur, sed etiam cum per eos quid in corpore operatur; quia nulla mens finita corpus, quod immotum est solo nutu voluntatis suæ in motum ponere, adeoque motum, qui non erat in rerum natura, producere potest, hoc enim solius Dei est. Sed omne id, quod mentes finitæ in corpore quodam efficere possunt, eo absolvitur, quod motus, quos in corporibus jam inveniunt; varie dirigere, eoque pacto infinitas rerum species efficere queunt.
units.tr: Second, the motion of the animal spirits in no way depends on the mind, insofar as it is simply motion, nor is it produced by the mind. This holds not only when something is represented to the mind through them, but also when something is effected in the body through them. For no finite mind can set a body that is at rest into motion by the mere nod of its will, and so produce a motion that did not exist in nature; this belongs to God alone. But everything that finite minds can effect in a certain body comes down to this: they variously direct the motions which they already find in bodies, and in this way they can bring about infinite kinds of things.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Directio hæc motuum islorum etiam non aliter, quàm per nutum voluntatis fit, quandoquidem (juxta th. 1. & 2.) mentes nullum localem motum, quo corpora movere possent, in se habent, multò minus manus, pedes & corporeum quodcunque, quo agant. Neque hoc negari debet ob id, quia non assequimur modum, quo simplex nutus voluntatis in corpora agat, hoc enim nec de Deo, nec de mente nostra nobis constat, de quibus tamen certissimum est, eos per contactum corporeum nihil agere. Et sane absurdum foret, negari illa, quæ clare distincte jam à nobis perspecta sunt, propter ea quæ nondum percepimus
units.tr: This direction of those motions also is effected only by a nod of the will, since (according to theses 1 and 2) minds have no local motion by which they could move bodies, much less hands, feet or any bodily thing by which they might act. Nor should this be denied on the ground that we do not grasp the manner in which a simple nod of the will acts on bodies. For this is known neither about God nor about our own mind, yet it is most certain that they do nothing through bodily contact. And indeed it would be absurd to deny those things which we have already clearly and distinctly perceived, on account of those things which we have not yet grasped.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Ex quibus denuo liquidè patet, quòd nulla mens finita quid supra vires Naturæ, multò minus contra leges Naturæ, materiæ, motibusque à Deo ipso positas, & juxta quas omnia in mundo fiunt, quasque nulla creatura invertere potest, producere possit. Ac idcirco quicquid unquam mentes finitæ possunt corporibus varietatum inducere, hoc juxta illas leges fieri certum est, quamvis modus, quo fiat, sæpissime nobis lateat. Quod sané mirum non est, cum innumera sint hominum opera, quæ rudiores, illorum causas nullo modo attingentes, præstigia & artes Diabolicas esse dicerent.
units.tr: From these things it is again plainly evident that no finite mind can produce anything beyond the powers of Nature, much less anything against the laws of Nature, of matter and of motion, which God himself has established and according to which all things in the world happen, and which no creature can overturn. Therefore, whatever changes finite minds can ever induce in bodies, it is certain that these happen according to those laws, although the manner in which they happen is very often hidden from us. This is hardly surprising, since there are countless human works whose causes cruder people do not grasp in any way, and who would therefore call them tricks and Diabolical arts.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Sed ut ad rem ipsam deveniamus; quis dubitabit, quòd, si manifestâ experientiâ convicti fateri debeamus, quædam à mente aliqua finita facta esse, quæ nostrum intellectum multis parasangis superant, illa hoc ipso non so- lùm lum potentiâ, sed etiam scientiâ mentem nostram excellat? Sed an dentur mentes quaedam nostrâ quidem intellectu & potentiâ multo majores, attamen finitæ; quæ ab omni mole corporea naturaliter sint separatæ, hoc est, quæ ab initio suæ creationis cum nullo corpore conjunctæ fuerint, cum quo ob immediatum talem nexum, qualis in homine est, unum quid compositum effecerint, uno nomine, an dentur Angeli, seu boni, seu mali, ab illis omnibus, qui Sacram Scripturam aut parvi faciunt, aut saltem ejus sensum & loquendi de hisce Geniis formam invertunt, aut saltem contradicendi studio se oblectantes ipsum solum Naturæ lumen ut arbitrum eligunt, interimque manifestam experientiam ab aliis relatam, non admittunt, in dubium trahi potest.
units.tr: But to come to the matter itself: who will doubt that, if manifest experience compels us to confess that certain things have been done by some finite mind which far surpass our understanding by many parasangs, that mind by this very fact excels ours not only in power but also in knowledge? But whether there are certain minds, indeed much greater than ours in understanding and power, yet finite, which are naturally separated from all corporeal mass, that is, which from the beginning of their creation were joined to no body, with which, through an immediate bond such as exists in man, they would have formed one composite thing, in one word, whether there are angels, whether good or bad, can be called into doubt by all those who either hold Sacred Scripture of little worth, or at least distort its sense and its manner of speaking about these spirits, or who, delighting in the mere love of contradiction, choose the light of Nature alone as arbiter and meanwhile do not admit manifest experience reported by others.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Ne igitur cum his longiorem confli­ctum ineuntes nos detineamus, ad no­strum institutum sufficit. 1. Quod à priore facilé queat demonstrari, ejus& shy;modi mentes innumeras, easque persectionum gradibus innumeris discrepantes, potuisse creari. 2. quod etiam illis qui omnem experientiam non negant, à posteriore probari queat, revera & actu malos Angelos dari.
units.tr: Therefore, so as not to detain ourselves by entering a longer contest with these men, what we have set out to do is sufficient. (1) That it can easily be demonstrated a priori that innumerable minds of this kind, differing from one another in innumerable degrees of perfection, could have been created. (2) That it can also be proved a posteriori, for those who do not deny all experience, that evil angels really and actually exist.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Saltem jam sufficiat nobis, per nudam hypothesin assumere Angelos tam bonos quam malos esse. Et de malis in specie nobis propositum est hisce Exercitationibus tractare, ut quidnam ex Dei vel jussu, vel conniventia per corpora operari, & quo modo in illa potentiam suam exercere, multaque mira producere queant, quantum caligantis ingenii nostri acies assequi poterit, scrutemur, quò vel hoc ipso, summa illorum impotentia, si nihil Deus eis permittat, manifesta fiat, & quàm parum metuendi sint illis, qui Deo suo constante fide arctissimè adhaerent.
units.tr: It is therefore enough for us, for the present, to assume by bare hypothesis that the angels are both good and bad. Our purpose in these Exercitations is to treat specifically of the bad ones: to examine, as far as the keenness of our dim understanding can reach, what they can accomplish through bodies, whether by the command or the permission of God, how they exercise their power in them, and what marvels they can produce; so that, by this very means, their utter powerlessness, should God permit them nothing, may be made plain, and how little they are to be feared by those who cling most closely to their God with steadfast faith.

units.la: CAP. II. DE ANGELORUM MALORUM NATURA. I.
units.tr: CAP. II. ON THE NATURE OF THE EVIL ANGELS. I.

units.la: HIS igitur præmissis, quid nam per Angelum vel potiùs Genium malum intelligamus, primò videndum erit. Nimirum Mentem finitam, ab omni corporis consortio naturaliter liberam; intellectus acumine & præstantiâ, non minus voluntatis efficacia humanas Mentes longe superantem; at vice versa ejusdem voluntatis summa malitia, & perversitate, innumeris gradibus & modis inferiorem.
units.tr: Having laid down these things, we must first consider what we mean by an evil angel, or rather evil genius. Namely, a finite mind, naturally free from all association with a body; surpassing human minds by far in the keenness and excellence of its intellect, and no less in the efficacy of its will; but on the contrary, inferior in countless degrees and ways in the extreme malice and perversity of that same will.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Mentem dicimus esse, adeoque de illa omne id, quod generaliter de omnibus mentibus finitis cap. præced. diximus affirmari etiam potest, quo pacto declinabimus præjudicium vulgatissimum, quo, sicuti omnes mentes, sic malum Genium non tantum ut spiritum corporeum imaginantur; sed ipsi etiam infinitas figuras monstrorum terrestrium, volatilium, aquatiliumque &c: affingunt. Saltem si sub forma hujus & illius substantiæ corporeæ appareat, hanc ad ejus naturam pertinere, sibi persuadent. Quin imò aliqui tam rudes sunt, ut omnino putent Angelos malos revera certam aliquam formam monstrosam habere, in qua obambulent & circumeant totam terram, & per illud corpus monstrosum videre, audire, loqui, devorare, destruere, erigere: uno nomine, omnia agere posse, sicut nos per nostrum corpus; at solùm Dei benignitate tate nostros oculos quasi teneri, ne illos videamus. Tales in papatu innumeros simplices invenies, quia homini& shy;bus misellis purgatorii & gehennæ cruciatus per ejusmodi monstra obtru& shy;ditur, & ad oculum dépingitur.
units.tr: We say that it is a mind, and therefore everything that we said generally of all finite minds in the preceding chapter can also be affirmed of it. By this we shall avoid the very common prejudice by which people imagine the evil genius, as well as all minds, not merely as a bodily spirit, but also attribute to it countless shapes of earthly monsters, of birds, of sea creatures, and so on. At least if it appears under the form of this or that corporeal substance, they persuade themselves that this belongs to its nature. Indeed some are so crude that they altogether think the evil angels really have some monstrous shape, in which they walk about and go round the whole earth, and through that monstrous body see, hear, speak, devour, destroy, and erect; in a word, that they can do all things as we do through our body, but that only by God's kindness are our eyes, as it were, held back, so that we do not see them. You will find countless simple folk of this kind among the Papists, because the wretched people are beaten with the torments of purgatory and hell through such monsters and have them painted before their eyes.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Finitam quoque dicimus ; ac ob id illi præsertim denegamus. 1. Omni­scientiam, sic ut nec absolutè intima nostra cogitata scire possit, hoc enim solius Dei esse, quia nostras Mentes omni momento reproducit, judica& shy;mus ; nec etiam alia arcaniora, quæ in mundo sunt fiuntque,ut hominum con& shy;silia, & similia; nisi Deus hæc illi aut& shy;revelet, aut permittat ex diversis cirt cumstantiis, quid homines cogitent au factûri sint, concludere, idque vel to­taliter, vel solùm ex parte; certò aut solùm probabiliter. 2. Ubique-præsen­tiam. Deus enim solus omnia operatur in omnibus, at malus Genius extra se nihil & nullibi operatur, nisi aut jussu aut conniventiâ Dei (juxta c. 1. §. 3.) Nullo enim alio modo præ­sentiam mentium, quàm per earum operationes concipi posse, ex dictis cap. præced liquidé. satis attendenti constabit. 3. Omnipotentiam, Deus enim solus exequitur illa quæ vult, & eo modo quo vult, Angelus verò malus non potest omne illud efficere,quod vult, sed solùm, quod licet, & ipsi à Deo permittitur. Nam si contra hanc summam Majestatem Voluntatem & Potentiam quid efficere posset, non esset mens finita & dependens à Deo, sed Deo major , quod est contradictorium.
units.tr: We also call it finite, and for this reason we especially deny it: (1) omniscience, so that it cannot know even our innermost thoughts absolutely, for we judge this to belong to God alone, since he re-creates our minds at every moment; nor can it know other more hidden things that are in the world and happen, such as the counsels of men and the like, unless God either reveals these to it, or permits it to conclude from various circumstances what men are thinking or are about to do, and this either wholly or only in part, with certainty or only with probability. (2) Presence everywhere. For God alone works all things in all things, whereas the evil genius works nothing outside itself and nowhere, except by the command or the permission of God (according to chapter 1, §3). For, as anyone who attends carefully to what was said in the preceding chapter will clearly see, the presence of minds can be conceived in no other way than through their operations. (3) Omnipotence. For God alone carries out what he wills, and in the way he wills, whereas the evil angel cannot bring about everything that it wills, but only what is lawful and what is permitted to it by God. For if it could effect anything against this supreme Majesty, Will and Power, it would not be a finite mind dependent on God, but greater than God, which is a contradiction.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Ex finita hac Genii hujus mali natura facilé igitur concludimus, quòd, si multi dentur tales Genii mali (uti innumeros dari posse quis dubitat?) gradus perfectionum inter illos quoque dari possint , adeòquc esse magis vel minùs scientes & potentes , prout Deus uni plus intelleƈtûs & potentiæ concedit , quàm aliis ; imò ipsorum scientiam indies accrescere. Nam ex hoc solo , quòd ut finitum quid concipimus , consequitur necessariò fines ejus magis extendi vel contrahi posse ; uti é contrario , quia in Deo nullus finis intelligibilis est , nec actu existit , illi etiam nil addi , nil detrahi potest. Quid mirum igitur , si throni , Majestates &c. in S. S. nominentur?
units.tr: From this finite nature of the evil genius we therefore easily conclude that, if many such evil genii are given (who doubts that countless ones can be?), degrees of perfection can also be found among them, and so they can be more or less knowing and powerful, according as God grants more intellect and power to one than to another; indeed their knowledge increases daily. For from this alone, that we conceive of it as something finite, it necessarily follows that its limits can be extended or contracted more; whereas on the contrary, since in God there is no intelligible limit and none actually exists, nothing can be added to him or taken from him. What wonder, then, if thrones, majesties and so on are named in Holy Scripture?

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Porrò dicimus Mentem hanc esse ab omni corporis consortio liberam & quidem dem naturaliter. Hoc est, non solùm quòd nîl corporei, in ejus essentia inveniatur, sed etiam quod non à Natura, hoc est, ab ipso Deo sit juncta immediaté corpori alicui, uti nostra Mens, idque à primo ejus creationis suæ puncto, sic ut unum quid cum eo constituat; sed quòd Deus voluerit, ut ad ejus naturam pertineat ab omni corporis consortio esse liberam, & indifferentem ut jungatur cum quocunque, juxta illa, quæ cap. I. §. I. &c. dicta sunt.
units.tr: Furthermore we say that this mind is free from all association with a body, and indeed naturally so. That is, not only is nothing corporeal to be found in its essence, but also it is not joined by nature, that is, by God himself, immediately to any body, as our mind is, and that from the very first point of its creation, so that it would make one thing with it; rather God willed that it should belong to its nature to be free from all association with a body, and indifferent so as to be joined to whatever, according to what was said in chapter 1, §1 etc.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Concedimus tamen, quòd intellectus acumine & prastantia Mentes humanas longé superet, hoc enim 1. ex ejus natura fluit, quia est ab omni corporis consortio libera. Nam plus quàm vellent experiuntur homines, qui ea, qua decet via in cognitione rerum progredi conantur, quantum hoc corporis consortium illis impedimentum afferat; quàm facilé à melioribus conceptibus per illud avocentur, quoties nos sensus fallant ; quoties memoria destituat &c: sic ut fateri debeant, se à præjudiciis sensuum seductos, non potuisse scientiam solidam, quæ ultra nomina & quòd de rerum qualitatibus juxta sensum perceptiones dicitur, se extendat, acquirere; hinc si cortice hoc relicto ipsam medullam attingere velint, debere mentem suam a corporis consortio quasi liberare, & sola puri intellectus acie ad intimas rerum naturas penetrare. Experiuntur autem hoc corporis impedimentum maxime, cum se supra illud, quod mundanum & corporeum est elevare, & vel Deum, vel mentem suam, vel aeterna gaudia & similia, sicuti sunt, pura mente concipere annituntur. 2. Huc multum facere potest, quod non, uti mens nostra uni corpori solum alligata est, sed succesivé jam his, jam illis, imo multis simul se jungere possit. (juxta c. 1. th. 1.) 3 Nec minus, quod, si concipiantur innumerae Mentes tales, possint sibi invicem facillime & citissime omne quod sciunt, & quicquid de rebus quibuscunque ulterius addiderunt, communicare. Hunc enim in finem non indigent voce, nec scripto, nec itinere & similibus adminiculis, quae longum tempus requirunt, sed haec sibi invicem communicant simplici revelatione suorum conceptuum; modo quidem nobis, hac in vita saltem, inconceptibili, attamen certo quia nil corporeum in iis agnoscimus (juxta th. 2. hujus) quamvis non videatur implicare. ut etiam adminîculs corporeis uti possint, uti de eo inferius quid attingemus. Sed cur uterentur, cùm melius id absque his possint? 4. Taceo, quòd jam a principio Mundi summa cupiditate flagrárint penetrandi in abditissima quæque Dei ejusque operum,nec ullam occasionem (ut sic loquar) elabi sinentes, tot seculorum spatio indefinita addiscere & experientiam diffusissimam acquirere potuerint. Hoc enim maximé earum interest, ad se suaque opera stabilienda.
units.tr: We do concede, however, that the keenness and excellence of its intellect far surpasses human minds. For this flows (1) from its nature, because it is free from all association with a body. For men experience more than they would wish, when they try to advance in the knowledge of things by the proper method, how greatly this association with the body hinders them; how easily they are turned aside through it from better conceptions whenever the senses deceive us; whenever memory fails them, and so on; so that they must confess that, led astray by the prejudices of the senses, they have not been able to acquire solid knowledge, which extends beyond names and beyond what is said of the qualities of things according to sensory perceptions; hence, if they wish to reach the very marrow once this husk is left behind, they must, as it were, free their mind from association with the body and penetrate to the inner natures of things by the keen edge of pure intellect alone. They experience this hindrance of the body most of all when they strive to raise themselves above what is worldly and corporeal, and to conceive by pure mind God, or their own mind, or eternal joys and similar things, as they are. (2) Much to the point is that our mind is not, as ours is, bound to one body only, but can join itself successively now to this, now to that, indeed to many at once (according to chapter 1, thesis 1). (3) No less is it that, if countless minds of this kind are conceived, they can very easily and very quickly communicate to one another everything they know, and whatever further they have added about any things whatever. For to this end they need neither voice, nor writing, nor travel, nor similar aids, which require a long time, but they communicate these things to one another by the simple revelation of their conceptions; in this life, at least, this is inconceivable to us, yet certain, since we recognise nothing corporeal in them (according to thesis 2 of this chapter), although it does not seem to involve a contradiction. That they could also use corporeal aids, we shall touch on further below. But why would they use them, when they can do better without these? (4) I say nothing of the fact that from the beginning of the world they have burned with the greatest desire to penetrate into the most hidden things of God and his works, and, letting no opportunity (so to speak) slip away, they have been able to learn an indefinite amount and acquire the widest experience over the span of so many ages. For this is especially to their advantage, in order to establish themselves and their works.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Insuper ei, ipsique similibus Mentibus denegare non possumus voluntatis quoque effic ciam nostra multo majorem, ob eandem scil: caulam, quòd non ut mentes nostrae uni corpori solum alligatæ sint, & in eo, & per illud solum operari debeant, sed simplici nutu voluntatis (hoc enim & non alio modo Mentes extra se quid operari excapit. 1. §. 2. 10. disces) in quaevis corpora agere possint, quia Deus Mentes has liberas reliquit. Ipsaque intellectus praestantia hîc plurimum adjuvat, uti notum est, quòd etiam homines, qui sunt ingeniosiores plura & admirabiliora in corpore suo, tùm mediante illo, in aliis corporibus producere valeant. Saltem experientia manifesta hoc docet illos, qui illam admittunt.
units.tr: Moreover, we cannot deny that such minds, and those like them, have a power of will much greater than ours, for the same reason: that our minds are not bound to one body only, to operate in it and through it alone, but by a simple nod of the will (for minds can effect something outside themselves in no other way, as you will learn from 1. §. 2. 10.) they can act upon any bodies whatsoever, because God has left these minds free. Their very excellence of intellect helps greatly here, as is well known: even men who are more gifted produce many and more admirable things in other bodies through their own body. At least manifest experience teaches this to those who admit it.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Vice versâ tamen hoc unico mentibus humanis multò inferiorem esse, asserimus, quòd in ejus voluntate sit summa, imò forsan nulli mortalium conceptibilis malitia & perversitas; quæ turpissima nigredo omnem reliquarum perfectionum splendorem tollit, facitque ut ob turpissimam (ut sic loquar) hanc turpidinem rerum omnium horribilissima & odio dignissima fiat. Perversitatem igitur hanc, cùm respectu intellectûs nostri indefinita esse videatur, mirum non est, quòd totaliter & propriis suis omnibusque indiciis particulatim describere non possimus; Imò licèt possemus, operæ pretium hîc esse non judicaremus, ideòque sufficiat paucis turpissimam hanc quasi Bestiam depingere.
units.tr: On the other hand, we assert that they are far inferior to human minds in this one respect: that in their will there is supreme, perhaps to no mortal conceivable, malice and perversity. This most shameful blackness takes away the splendour of all their other perfections, and makes them, on account of this most shameful (so to speak) foulness, the most horrible and most worthy of hatred of all things. Since this perversity, in comparison with our intellect, seems to be unlimited, it is no wonder that we cannot describe it fully and particularly in all its features and signs. Indeed, even if we could, we would not judge it worth the effort here; therefore let it suffice to paint this most shameful beast, as it were, in a few strokes.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Concipimus igitur illam in hoc confistere, quòd etsi hic malus Genius clarissimè & distinctissimè cognoscat Summum illud Bonum, à quo creatus est, & omne quod perfectionis habet, absque ullo merito suo accepit, agnoscatque hoc ut verissimum; imò se teneri ob id illi Creatori & Patri suo se totum ad ejus laudes & officia cum omnibus tradere, & quantum in se est, ejus gloriam per reliquas creaturas etjam promovere &c. Uno nomine, Deum esse omnia in omnibus, & ad eum tanquam Summum Bonum omnia spectare, & referri debere, sic ut simile huic nec quid sit, nec esse possit &c; Quod inquam, etsi haec omnia distincte cognoscat, & ut verissima agnoscat, attamen abjurato quasi omni naturae lumine, & propria conscientia & judicio contradicenti, nihilominus se isti Creatori suo subjicere noluerit, sed rebellis factus, nullo impulsus corporis stimulo, nullaque vel tantillum probabili ratione, sed simpliciter, quia voluit, similem cum Deo gloriam impudentissime & stultissime affectârit. Hinc ingratissimorum ingratissimus & pessimorum pessimus redditus, à Deo rejectus, & ab ejus gratia aeternum exclusus respicere non potest; Quapropter desperatione continuâ & morsu conscientiae incomprehensibili nunquam non cruciatus, Dei & reliquarum Creaturarum odio intensissimo flagrat, adeoque quicquid vitiorum concipi potest, loco Dei pro Summo Bono habet, ac omne quod ullo mo-
units.tr: We conceive, then, that it consists in this: although this evil spirit knows most clearly and distinctly the highest Good from whom he was created, and acknowledges that he has received everything of perfection that he possesses without any merit of his own, and acknowledges this as most true; indeed, that he is bound on that account to surrender himself wholly, with all that he is, to his Creator and Father, for his praises and duties, and as far as in him lies to promote his glory also through the other creatures, etc. In a word, that God is all in all, and that all things look to Him as the highest Good and ought to be referred to Him, so that nothing similar to this either is or can be, etc.; yet although he knows all these things distinctly and acknowledges them as most true, nevertheless, having as it were abjured every light of nature, and contrary to his own conscience and judgment, he has been unwilling to submit himself to this Creator of his. Having become rebellious, impelled by no sting of the body, and by no even slightly probable reason, but simply because he willed it, he has most shamelessly and most foolishly aspired to a glory like God's. Hence, having become the most ungrateful of the ungrateful and the worst of the worst, rejected by God and excluded eternally from His grace, he cannot look back; therefore, always tormented by continual despair and by an incomprehensible gnawing of conscience, he burns with the most intense hatred of God and of the other creatures. And so he holds as his highest Good, in place of God, whatever kind of vice can be conceived, and whatever he can in any way bring about against the kingdom of God and the salvation of the remaining creatures, God permitting him, he carries out with the greatest delight, because he can conceive nothing more fitting to himself and more worthy of his nature.

units.la: { * } Pag. 27 ends mid-word; the line continues on the next page. do contra Dei regnum & creaturarum reliquarum salutem efficere ipsi Deus concedit, summâ cum voluptate patrat; quia nil sibi convenientius & suâ indole dignius concipere potest.
units.tr: Whatever he can do against the kingdom of God and the salvation of the other creatures, which God permits him to do, he carries out with the greatest delight, because he can conceive nothing more fitting for himself or more worthy of his nature.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Talis igitur Genius malus, aut potius innumerabiles tales (quia probabile satis est ipso naturæ lumine, quòd quemadodum in omni rebellione fit, multi defecerint, à Duce & authore illius factionis in consortium culpæ & solatium poenæ contracti) tales, inquam, Genii mali, si igitur ponantur in rerum natura existere, quidnam in corpora & per corpora efficere valeant Deo ipsis libertatem concedente (juxta th. 3. c. 1.) indagandum erit.
units.tr: Such an evil spirit, or rather innumerable such evil spirits (since it is quite probable, by the very light of nature, that, as happens in every rebellion, many have defected, and have been drawn into fellowship of guilt and comfort in punishment by the leader and author of that faction), such evil spirits, I say, if they are supposed to exist in the nature of things, what they can effect in and through bodies, God granting them freedom (according to th. 3, c. 1), is what we must now inquire into.

units.la: CAP. III. De potentia malorum Angelorum in corpora Generaliter.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. On the power of the evil angels over bodies in general.

units.la: Corpora quæ ministerio Diaboli inservire apta sunt, in genere quidem sunt omnia fluida, quia motum inse jam habent, extra quem nihil efficiet, ciet, juxta C. I. §. 10. at præsertim ipsi inservit aër, unde merito Dominator in aëre vel Princeps aëris, cujus nutui & arbitrio aër obtemperat, vocatur. Per aërem verò intelligimus id omne, quod in eo continetur, sic ut præter id, quod ad nativum aërem pertinet, etiam vapores & exhalationes multivariæ, & præsertim materia ignis & cœlestis illa, quæ lucis subjectum est, ad eum referatur. Nam quia mixtura hæc summé heterogenea est, tum subtilissima variisque motibus nunquam non agitata, ipsi præ aliis inservit ad scenas suas in infinitum variandas.
units.tr: The bodies that are fit to serve the devil's ministry are, in general, all fluids, since they already have motion in themselves, beyond which they can effect and stir nothing, according to Ch. 1, §10. But above all the air serves him, whence he is rightly called Lord of the air or Prince of the air, since the air obeys his nod and will. By air, however, we mean everything that is contained in it, so that, besides what belongs to the air in its natural state, the many kinds of vapours and exhalations are also included, and especially the matter of fire and that heavenly matter which is the subject of light. For since this mixture is most highly heterogeneous, and is also very subtle and never ceases to be moved by various motions, it serves him better than others for varying his scenes without end.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Cùmque nullum particulare corpus in terra inveniatur, per quod non vel hæc omnis mixtura aëris transeat, vel quod in ea subtilius est, & præ aliis materia cœlestis cum materia ignis, vel ad minimum sola materia ignis, quæ per nullum non corpus copiâ satis magnâ continuò ruit, omnium admirabilium, quæ in corporibus fiunt causa efficiens principalior est, mirum non est, quòd etiam per totum terrarum orbem tam infra quàm supra terram, in omnis generis corpora vim suam exercere possit. Atque id maximé, quod concipiamus in medio terræ Oceanum quasi ignis purissimi latè extensum æstuare, ex quo, si non flumina, saltem rivuli &c, ad minimum effluvia continua per omnes terræ partes, (uti sanguis & spiritus, ex corde per omnia nostra membra) indesinenter distribuuntur, illasque calefaciunt, fovent & vegetant, sic ut ubique in terra inveniat aptissimum instrumentum, quo in infinitum hic mille artifex opera sua variare potest. Hinc & Deus, Princeps & Dominus hujus mundi, vel ævi, id est, hujus terræ hoc nomine dici potest, qui sibi (quamvis impudentissimè) omnia regna mundi ejusque thesauros adscribit, & potens est in filiis inobedientiæ vel hujus mundi per hæc opera sua, quibus eos ludit & illudit.
units.tr: Since no particular body is found on earth through which this whole mixture of air does not pass, or what in it is subtlest, and above all the heavenly matter together with the matter of fire, or at least the matter of fire alone, which flows without cease through every body in sufficiently great quantity, it is no wonder that he can exercise his power over bodies of every kind throughout the whole globe, both below and above the earth. This is especially so if we suppose that in the middle of the earth an ocean of purest fire, widely extended, seethes, from which, if not rivers, at least streams and, at the very least, continual effluvia are distributed without interruption through all parts of the earth (as blood and spirits are from the heart through all our limbs), warming, cherishing and quickening them, so that everywhere on earth he finds a most apt instrument by which this thousand-handed artificer can vary his works without end. Hence also God may be called by this name Prince and Lord of this world, or of this age, that is, of this earth, who ascribes to himself (though most shamelessly) all the kingdoms of the world and their treasures, and who is powerful over the sons of disobedience, or of this world, through these works of his, by which he mocks and deceives them.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Imò si rem penitius introspiciamus, quid absurdi sequeretur, si dicamus damnatum hunc Genium, non tantùm sic igni huic jungi, ut per eum operetur, uti mens nostra per spiritus animales, sed etiam per ignem hunc, ipsi omnibusque damnatis à principio mundi jam paratum, pati, sicuti mens nostra etiam ultimò & immediatè per spiritus animales patitur; quippe in utroque mentium finitarum conjunctio
units.tr: Indeed, if we look more deeply into the matter, what absurdity would follow if we say that this damned Genius is joined to this fire not only so that he works through it, as our mind works through the animal spirits, but also that he suffers through this fire, which has been prepared for him and for all the damned since the beginning of the world, just as our mind also suffers, ultimately and immediately, through the animal spirits? For in both cases there is a union of finite minds

units.la: Note: the signature-like catchword "ctio" appears at the foot right. Actio cum corporibus potest consistere juxta c. 1. §2. Porrò, quia per passiones animæ, quas mens ob conjunctionem corporis habet, non solùm intelligitur dolor, vel injucunda & tristis illa animæ perceptio, quæ planè diversa est à motu spirituum, illum menti nostræ, aut ignis, illum Diabolo, repræsentante, sed etiam intelligatur generaliter omnis perceptio, ut colorum, lucis, sonorum, verborum &c: num repugnat Genios malos posse sibi invicem per hæc corpora, quæ nutui illorum, inserviunt, multa citissimè communicare, & quasi mediantibus illis, colloqui, & similia facere.
units.tr: Note: the catchword "ctio" appears at the foot on the right, in the manner of a signature. Action can coexist with bodies, according to Ch. 1, §2. Moreover, since by the passions of the soul, which the mind has because of its union with the body, is understood not only pain, or that unpleasant and sad perception of the soul, which is plainly different from the motion of the spirits, the one presenting itself to our mind, the other to the devil, but also is generally understood every perception, such as of colours, light, sounds, words and so on, is there any contradiction in the evil Genii being able to communicate to one another many things very swiftly through these bodies, which serve their nod, and, as it were, by means of them to converse and do similar things?

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Quo posito liquet, quòd veluti mens nostra immediatè suam vim in corpus suum mediantibus spiritibus animalibus exercet, quos ex cerebri ventriculis tanquam ex receptaculo naturali ad corporis partes citissimè ablegat, eisque varia in corpore suo operatur, sic Dominus hîc perversi orbis ex throno quasi sui regni, hoc est, igne ille in medio terræ perpetuo flagrante (quique olim comburet terram, quæ per peccata hominum vanitatibus subjecta est, ex qua effodiuntur opes, quæ sunt malorum irritamenta, &, uno nomine, instrumentum est omnis nequitiæ) possit magnam illius partem citissimè ad has & illas terræ partes amandare, illaque mediante innumera tam in terræ viscceribus, quàm in ejus superficie producere.
units.tr: This being laid down, it is clear that just as our mind exercises its power immediately over its body by means of the animal spirits, which it sends most swiftly from the cavities of the brain, as from a natural receptacle, to the parts of the body, and by them works various effects in its body, so the Lord of this perverse world from the throne of his kingdom, that is, from that fire ever burning in the middle of the earth (which will one day burn up the earth that is subjected to vanities through the sins of men, from which riches are dug up that are incitements to evil, and which, in a word, is the instrument of all wickedness), can send a great part of it very swiftly to these and those parts of the earth, and through it produce countless effects both in the bowels of the earth and on its surface.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Firmiter tamen statui posse videtur malum Genium mente nostra in hoc inferiorem esse, quòd non pro lubitu & quoties vult per hæc corpora agere possit, uti mens nostro si modò illud sit bene dispositum. Nam ex jam dictis patet, quòd talis nexus naturalis inter quodcunque corpus, & inter malum Genium non sit, adeoque se toties solum eis jungere queat, quoties Deus hoc aut jubet eoque utitur, vel tanquam carnifice suo & exequutore voluntatis & justitiæ suæ ut homines cruciet, seu quoad corpus solùm, seu quoad mentem solam, seu quoad utrumque, vel tanquam instrumento quodam, quo fides hominum, ejusque constantia probatur, aut in quemcunque tandem finem hanc conjunctionem ipsi permittit. Si enim toties, quoties ipsi liberet, uti corporibus possfet, ad suam voluntatem exequendam, nunquam non abutcretur, imò exiguo tempore omnia perderet, confunderet, tota-mque rerum naturam destrueret, aliamque conderet, sicque se ejus Dominum & authorem plenarium constitueret. Præsertim v. genus humanum perderet, & maxime quoad mentem, quam (quia ad instar sui plane eam deturpare & secum ex Dei gratia totaliter exturbare non potuit, & ob id ringitur) plane inverteret & ad suam imaginem reformaret, ut id ex C. 2. th. 9. sequitur.
units.tr: Yet it seems that it can be firmly held that the evil Genius is in this respect inferior to our mind: he cannot act through these bodies at his pleasure and whenever he wishes, as our mind can, provided it is itself well disposed. For from what has been said it is plain that there is no natural bond between any body and the evil Genius, and so he can join himself to them only as often as God either commands this, or makes use of him, either as his executioner and the agent of his will and justice, to torment men, whether in body only, or in mind only, or in both, or as an instrument by which the faith of men and its constancy are tested, or finally permits him this union for whatever end. For if he could make use of bodies whenever it pleased him, to carry out his own will, he would never cease to abuse them, and indeed in a short time he would destroy and confound everything, and would destroy the whole order of nature and found another, and so constitute himself its full lord and author. Above all he would destroy the human race, and especially as regards the mind, which (since he could not wholly deface it after his own likeness and wholly cast it out of God's grace, and is therefore raging) he would utterly overturn and reshape into his own image, as follows from Ch. 2, Th. 9.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Mirandum igitur nullo modo est, quod ob infinitam Dei misericordiam non permittentem, ut semper voluntatem suam exequatur, rarius hominibus nocere possit, uti etiam mirandum non est, quod si illam exequatur, id fiat præ aliis in filiis infidelitatis & inobedientiæ, in quibus potens est hic Dominus tenebrarum; atque ob id spectra, veneficia & similia Diaboli opera 1. in illis locis frequentius observentur, ubi Verus & Triunus Deus non agnoscitur colituraque, uti inter barbaras gentes, quibus lux Evangelica non eluxit & latum illud nunc um de Redemtore suo nondum est annunciatum. 2. Inter Pontificios, qui se Christianos esse jactitent, attamen Deum Triunum non, uti decet, in Spiritu & Veritate adorant & colunt, sed cultu fictitio & idololatrico; quia omnia, quae de Deo, Patre, Filio & Spiritu S., quae de angelis; quae de aeterna vita aut morte concipiunt dicuntque corporum ad instar sibi repraesentant. Hinc continuis imaginationum ludibriis decepti, loco veri Dei idolum aliquod; loco angeli boni juvenem pulcherrimum; loco mali angeli monstrum; loco aeternae vitae, nescio quas nudas corporales voluptates; loco aeternae mortis cruciatus, carnificinae modo inferendos, cum poëtis & fabulonibus vigilantes somniant.
units.tr: It is therefore by no means surprising that, because of God's infinite mercy, which does not permit the evil one always to carry out his will, he can harm men only rarely; and it is likewise not surprising that, when he does carry it out, this happens chiefly among the sons of unbelief and disobedience, over whom this lord of darkness has power. Hence ghosts, witchcraft and similar works of the Devil are more frequently observed (1) in those places where the true and triune God is not known or worshipped, as among barbarous nations, to whom the light of the Gospel has not shone and to whom the joyful news of their Redeemer has not yet been announced; (2) among the Papists, who boast that they are Christians, yet do not adore and worship the triune God as is fitting, in spirit and in truth, but with a fictitious and idolatrous worship; for whatever they conceive and say about God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, about the angels, and about eternal life or death, they picture to themselves after the manner of bodies. Hence, deceived by the constant mockeries of their imaginations, they dream while awake, with the poets and fabulists, of some idol in place of the true God, of a most beautiful youth in place of the good angel, of a monster in place of the evil angel, of some sort of bare bodily pleasures in place of eternal life, and of torments of eternal death to be inflicted in the manner of butchery.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Non tamen negari potest, quod inter illos, qui hoc idololatrico cultu omnia non permiscuerunt, hanc suam potentiam Genius malus exercere non poterit. Nam 1. etsi Deum non in imagine aut per eam adorent, informenturque satis, Dei regnum in potu & cibo & similibus non constiterre, & porro quae ad cultum Dei verum spectant, illos doceatur; attamen quotusquisque est (saltem inter illos, qui & viles sunt animo, nec solidioribus studiis exercitati) qui non a radicatis praejudiciis infantiae, omnia sibi sub imagine corporea repraesentantis, abripiatur ut se continere non possit, quin de Deo cogitans aut Angelo, aut simili quodam puré intelligibili, idolum aliquod loco ejus in cerebro per imagi-nationem erigat, juxta quod de rebus illis puré intelligibilibus judicet, loquatur que, imo ipsum Deum colat; itaque idololatriam subtilem committat? Hi igitur ex parte adhuc filii tenebrarum tum quasi sunt, qui non toto animo Deum suum admittunt, sed superstitionibus, vanisque conceptibus indulgentes aperiunt quasi fenestram, per quam malus Genius in illorum animos illabitur. Namque ad omnium homi-num mores actusque sagacissimé & accuratissimé attendens, hosque sibi paratos magis inveniens, præconceptas has opiniones, quantum in ipso est, fovet, & ut magis persuadeat, corporeos, quos de Deo ejusque operibus spiritualibus habent conceptus, esse bonos, sicque idololatriam hanc confirmet, suumque regnum magis in illis erigat, illorum imaginationi in contenplandis v.gr Diabolis, æternæ poenæ &c: succurrit, camque tam vividam facit, ut mente in eorum consideratione a'té desixa, illud quod in cerebro suo solum contemplantur, extra se vidisse, sub forma hujus aut illius, jurant idque spectrum esse dicant. Simili
units.tr: Yet it cannot be denied that among those who have not mixed up everything with this idolatrous worship, the evil Genius will not be able to exercise his power. For (1) although they do not worship God in an image or through one, and although they are sufficiently instructed that the kingdom of God does not consist in drink and food and the like, and are taught those things which pertain to the true worship of God, yet how few are there (at least among those who are base in mind and not trained in more solid studies) who are not carried away by the deep-rooted prejudices of infancy, which represent everything to them under a bodily image, so that they cannot refrain from thinking of God or of an angel, or of some similar purely intelligible thing, and from setting up in their brain, in place of it, some idol by imagination, according to which they judge, speak, and even worship God himself, and so commit a subtle idolatry? Such people, then, are still in some measure children of darkness, since they do not admit their God with their whole mind, but, indulging in superstitions and empty notions, they open, as it were, a window through which the evil Genius glides into their minds. For, attending most shrewdly and most carefully to the morals and actions of all men, and finding these more ready for him, he fosters these preconceived opinions as far as in him lies, and, that he may persuade more effectively, he makes the bodily conceptions they have of God and his spiritual works seem good; and so he confirms this idolatry and sets up his kingdom more firmly in them. When they contemplate, for example, devils or eternal punishment, he comes to the aid of their imagination and makes it so vivid that, with the mind fixed intently on their consideration, they swear that they have seen outside themselves, under the form of this or that, what they contemplate only in their own brain, and they say that it is a ghost. In a similar

units.la: modo ad iddolatriam, venefícia, aliasque artes diabolicas facilé tales incitabit. De modo quo hoc Diabolus faciat inferius. Et 2. Diabolus hanc fcenam suam adhuc faciliùs instruet & absolvet, quò animam alicujus viliorem & rerum divinarum, naturaliumque magis ignorantem inveniet. Talis enim cùm passionibus suis plané mancipata sit, divortiumque cum sana ratione fecerit, nihilque judicet, nisi quod passio præscns dictat, unde jam lætitiâ, jam tristitiâ; jam amore, jam odio; &c: per vices abripitur, & in suis judiciis est inconstantissima, occasionem hanc diabolus arripiens quassatam passionibus proprijs mentem ulteriùs quassare & cribrare quasi potest, imaginationibusque illius propriis (uti jam innuimus) abusus illam illudere. 3. Hucque multum facit temperamentum certum corporis, quòd quo magis hominem ad tristitiam, metum, terrorem & solitudinem disponit, & cum reliquis causis procatarcticis concurrit, eo omnium facilius Diabolus scopo suo potiri potest; uti inferius id clariùs ostendetur. Saltem experientia probat, quòd inter homines sapientes, in Dei & operum ejus cognitione satis versatos, tum cordatos & animo fortes, in ò audaces, rarisfi[catchword absent] rissimé quis inveniatur, qui spectrum viderit; at quòd melancholici, plebeculi, & præsertim sexus fœmineus illis præ aliis terreatur. Uti rarissimum quoque est, spectra à multis simul videri.
units.tr: way he will easily incite such people to idolatry, witchcraft and other diabolical arts. Concerning the manner in which the Devil does this, more will be said below. And (2) the Devil will prepare and complete this scene of his all the more easily when he finds a soul that is baser and more ignorant of divine and natural things. For such a person, being wholly enslaved to his passions and having divorced himself from sound reason, judges nothing except what the present passion dictates; hence he is carried off now by joy, now by sadness, now by love, now by hatred, and so on by turns, and is most inconstant in his judgments. Seizing this opportunity, the Devil can, as it were, further shake and sift a mind already shaken by its own passions, and mock it by abusing its own imaginations (as we have already hinted). (3) Moreover, a certain bodily temperament contributes much to this: the more it disposes a man to sadness, fear, terror and solitude, and concurs with the other preparatory causes, the more easily the Devil can attain his aim; as will be shown more clearly below. Experience at least proves that among wise men, well versed in the knowledge of God and his works, and also prudent and brave of spirit, and not bold, it is very rarely that anyone is found who has seen a ghost; but that melancholics, the common folk, and especially the female sex, are more terrified by them than others. It is likewise very rare for ghosts to be seen by many at the same time.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Quæ omnia ex eis, quæ jam particulariùs de potentia Geniorum malorum in corpora dicemus clariùs cognoscentur.
units.tr: All these things will be understood more clearly from what we shall now say in more detail about the power of the evil Genii over bodies.

units.la: (38) EXERCITATIONUM PHYSICARUM. De Angelorum Malorum in Corpo- ra Potentia. II.
units.tr: (38) EXERCITATIONUM PHYSICARUM. On the Power of Evil Angels in Bodies. II.

units.la: CAP. I. De Angelorum Malorum Potentia in COR- PORA extra nostrum posita.
units.tr: CHAP. I. On the Power of Evil Angels over Bodies outside us.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: GEneralioribus Exercitatione priore præmissis ad particulariorem potentiæ Angelorum malorum contemplationem descendamus. Sed hic se immensum theatrum multivariis illorum actionibus refertissimum aperit, quod non pauca nobis ostendit, quæ non solùm ingenii mei tenelli vires, sed etiam omnium hominum superant, si modum, quo illa à malis his Geniis patrantur indagare velimus, juxta c. I. §. 11. & II. §. 6. Exerc: I. Et quis de eo dubitaret, cùm satis constet, quod inter homines innumera stratagemata, tum artium actionumque varia genera tam secreta sint fiantque, ut vicinissimis etiam,
units.tr: Having set out the more general matters in the previous exercise, let us now descend to a closer contemplation of the power of evil angels. Here, however, there opens up an immense theatre, crowded with their manifold activities, which shows us many things that exceed not only the slender powers of my intellect but those of all men, if we wish to investigate the manner in which these things are carried out by the evil Genii, as stated in ch. I §11 and II §6 of Exercise I. And who would doubt it, since it is well established that among men there are countless stratagems and various kinds of arts and actions, so secret and so carried out that they lie hidden even from their closest, dearest and wisest friends?

units.la: amicissimis & sapientissimis lateant? Multò enim magis callidissimus Genius, qui artes decipiendi infinitas habet, cujusque omnia opera, sunt opera tenebrarum, hoc est, non solùm quòd sunt malitiâ plena, & tenebris fpiritualibus involuta, aut quòd eorum plurima de noctu,& in locis tenebricosis plurimum peragantur, sed maximè etiam, quòd tam subtilia sint; ut nec de die lynceis (quod ajunt) oculis videri queant, sua negotia occultabit. Quia tamen non sunt omnia æquè occulta, præsertim in quantum solùm confiderantur ut talia, quæ juxta leges naturæ fieri debent, (vide C. 1. §. 9) & non ut consilia & intentiones ejus, horum quædam præfenti Exercitatione considerationi nostræ subjiciemus.
units.tr: Much more, then, will the most crafty Genius, who has infinite arts of deception, and whose every work is a work of darkness, conceal his undertakings. This holds not only because his works are full of malice and wrapped in spiritual darkness, or because most of them are carried out by night and in dark places, but above all because they are so subtle that they cannot be seen even by day, not even with lynx eyes, as they say. Yet since not all of them are equally hidden, especially insofar as they are considered only as such things, which must come about according to the laws of nature (see ch. 1 §9), and not as his plans and intentions, we shall submit some of these to our consideration in the present exercise.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Ut autem hoc commodiûs fiat, a levioribus initium faciamus, quò ex eorum cognitione ad magis stupenda penetranda nos præparemus. Tum etiam, ne quis præjudicio detineatur, præmonere debemus, nos nîl aliud, quàm modum probabilem, quo hæc omnia à malo Genio fieri possint, proposituros, susque deque habentes, an eodem facta sint. Cum enim idem efsectus fecundum leges Naturæ univer-fa-
units.tr: So that this may be done more conveniently, let us begin with the lighter matters, so that from knowing them we may prepare ourselves to penetrate more astonishing things. Then too, lest anyone be held back by prejudice, we must forewarn that we shall propose nothing beyond a plausible mode by which all these things could be done by the evil Genius, and that we are indifferent as to whether they were in fact done in this way. For since the same effect is produced by nature and art in many different ways, according to the universal laws of nature,

units.la: sales multis diversis modis à Natura & Arte producantur, nemo inficias ibit, hoc multò Magis Genium, scientiâ suâ omnes homines superantem, præstiturum, nullumque, nisi ex illius revelatione, certò dicturum, quem præ aliis elegerit. Nostrum vero institutum ad hoc præcipuè collimat, ut aliquo modorum istorum probabili satis allato, quantumin nobis est præjudicium vulgatissimum & summè periculosum ex animis hominum exscindamus, quò putant malos Genios peculiari modo, & præter vel supernatural (ut loquuntur) hoc est, non eo, quo omnia in corporibus fiunt, at nescio quo excellentiore, hæc peragere.
units.tr: no one will deny that the Genius, who surpasses all men in his knowledge, will achieve this far more readily, and no one could say for certain, except from his revelation, which of these ways he has chosen over the others. Our purpose is aimed chiefly at this: that, once some sufficiently probable mode of these has been offered, we may root out, as far as lies in us, the most common and most dangerous prejudice from men's minds, by which they think that evil Genii carry out these things in a peculiar way, beyond or supernatural (as they put it), that is, not by that means by which everything in bodies happens, but by some I know not what more excellent means.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.
