units.la: Consideremus igitur primò quo modo in aëre, ut commodissimo suo elemento (ut ajunt) dominetur. Ex Physica liquet, quâ ratione aër quocunque modo in angustiam coactus, ex ea propulsus ventos exhibeat etiam validissimos, facillimè igitur apparet, quòd sicuti generaliores isti venti per obstantes nubes, montes, turres &c: necessario fiunt; & particulariores ab hominibus ope follis, æolipylæ, tubi, & oris flabelli &c: sic facilius malus Genius nuda suâ voluntate maximam copiam aëris versus unam partem, imò contrariam riam & fecundum quatuor cardines mundi, aut etiam citissime in gyrum, ut turbo fiat, propellere valet. (juxta illa quæ Exerc: 1. sunt dicta) Quo posito, quid mirum, si per illum ventum turres, templa, ædificia, horrea &c: dejicere; arbores, segetes prosternere, & eradicare, naufragia causare; fluctus ad littora pellendo aggeres perrumpere, itaque inundationem causare; imo ranas, pisces, aves, lapides, segetes, stramen, &c uno nomine omnia, quæ ventus hic potens est secum avehere, ex uno loco in aliam transportare, & similia infinita efficere valeat?
units.tr: Let us consider first how he rules in the air, as his most convenient element (as they say). It is clear from physics that when air is forced into a narrow space and driven out from it, it produces even very violent winds. It is therefore easily apparent that just as these more general winds arise necessarily through obstructing clouds, mountains, towers and so on, and the more particular winds are made by men with the help of bellows, an aeolipile, a tube, or a fan-mouthed instrument, and so on, in the same way the evil Genius, by his bare will, can more easily drive a great quantity of air towards one part, or even the opposite part, and according to the four quarters of the world, or even very swiftly in a circle, so that a whirlwind is formed (in accordance with what was said in Exercise I). Given this, what wonder if, through that wind, he is able to throw down towers, temples, buildings, granaries and so on; to lay low and uproot trees and crops; to cause shipwrecks; to break through dykes by driving waves against the shore, and so cause flooding; and indeed to carry frogs, fish, birds, stones, crops, straw, and, in a word, everything that this powerful wind can carry with it, from one place and transport it to another, and to effect countless similar things?

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Et quia inaëre innumeri semper sunt vapores & exhalationes, quæ si in unum cogantur nubes, pluviam, nivem, grandinemque componunt, quàm facilé ipsi ut vapores & exhalationes in tam densas nubes cogere, radiis solaribus objectæ media die tenebras inferant densissimas & palpabiles; aut quæ, prout variis figuris constant, diverlisque modis radios solares vel lunares ad terram & spectatorum oculos reflectunt & refringunt, similitudinem diversarum rerum quâ homines illudit, exhibent; aut si unæ in alias ab ipso deturbentur; aut versus montes, turresque &c; frangantur, fulgetra, fulmina & tonitrua excitabunt; quibus mediantibus arbores disrumpere; turres, ædificia, horrea, segetes &c: confringere & incendere; hominibusque & pecudi multis modis nocere poterit. Cùmque non solùm sciat, quomodo pluvia producatur, sed etiam quòd pro diversa exhalationum mixtura possit esse lactei, sanguinei, aliusque coloris; odores spirare non minus varios; tum infecta subtilia in aëre ex certis exhalationibus aut lapillos &c: prognata continere, quàm facilè talia pluviæ miscebit, & ita lac, sanguinem, atramentum, odores bonos malosque, infecta, lapillulos, & quasi aciculas &c: plucre faciet; aut ex pluvia ista ad varios suos usus desumet? similiter grandine non solùm maximo effecto hominibus brutisque plurima damna inferre potest, sed ad exemplar ingeniosæ Naturæ diversas figuras ipsi induere, ut vel crucem, vel conum, vel stellam, vel faciem quamcumvis referant, ut his figuris non minus ac speciebus illis in aere repræsentatis, credulitati hominum occultas insidias struat.
units.tr: And since in the air there are always countless vapours and exhalations, which, when gathered together into a cloud, form rain, snow and hail, how easily could he gather the vapours and exhalations into such dense clouds, which, placed before the rays of the sun, bring on the thickest and palpable darkness at midday; or which, taking on various shapes, reflect and refract the solar or lunar rays to the earth and to the eyes of onlookers, presenting the likeness of different things by which he deceives men; or, if he drives them against one another or against mountains, towers and so on, they will break and produce lightning, thunderbolts and thunder, by means of which he can tear apart trees, shatter and burn towers, buildings, granaries, crops and so on, and harm men and beasts in many ways. And since he knows not only how rain is produced, but also that, according to the different mixture of exhalations, it can be milky, bloody or of some other colour, and can breathe out odours no less varied, and that he can hold subtle infections in the air, or little stones and so on produced from certain exhalations, how easily will he mix such things into the rain, and so make milk, blood, ink, good and bad odours, infections, little stones and something like needles rain down; or take them from that rain for his various purposes? Similarly with hail: he can not only inflict very great harm on men and beasts, but, after the pattern of ingenious Nature, can also assume diverse shapes, so that they represent a cross, a cone, a star, or any face whatever, and so, by these figures no less than by those appearances represented in the air, he may lay hidden snares for the credulity of men.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Porrò, quia pro exhalationum harum infinita varietate diversæ speciei meteora generantur, ingeniosus hic artifex ad similitudinem illorum meteora quaevis alia producere novit, formas & figuras hominum, avium, plantarum, fasciculorum straminis ardentium &c: referentes, eaque pro libitu, vento ad hoc concitato ferre, ut circa flumina, sepulcra, carceres, patibula, locaque quaevis à frequentia hominum remota, ire, redire, saltare, obambulare, volare &c: videantur. Idque praesertim tempore pestis, justitiae publicè administratae &c: quò hominibus terrorem incutiat, cogitationesque superstitiosas ingerat; Unde etiam ista loca spectris, lemuribus, spiritibusque famosa esse dicuntur.
units.tr: Furthermore, since from this infinite variety of exhalations meteors of diverse kinds are generated, this ingenious artificer knows how to produce, in imitation of them, any other meteors whatever: forms and figures of men, birds, plants, bundles of burning straw, and so on, representing them, and to carry them at will with the wind set in motion for this purpose, so that they are seen to go, return, dance, wander about, fly, and so on, around rivers, graves, prisons, gallows, and any places remote from the throng of men. And this especially in a time of plague, or of justice publicly administered, and so on, so that he may strike terror into men and instil superstitious thoughts. Hence these places are also said to be notorious for specters, ghosts, and spirits.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Imò cum ab exhalationum varia attemperatione contagium in aëre possit oriri, quod pestem & mortem hominibus & pecudibus, uti sterilitatem inducat; tum segetibus arboribusque nocet; hoc ipso concitato, quid non damni humano generi inferet? Et cum naturaliter tempore talis pestis meteora praedicta frequentiora esse possint, ignesque fatui circa sepulchra haerere, quia ex eis exhalationum, peste extinctorum, copia est frequentior, illorum aliquos in unum compingens, ansam dat vilibus animabus spiritus ex sepulchro redeuntes & majorem pestem &c. indigitantes, & nescio quid non, singere. Et si forsan hoc tempore, cometa in cœlo fulgeat, quem vulgus sibi firmiter persuadet indicium instantis belli, pestis, famis, sterilitatisque certissimum esse, quas non curas & auxietates, quasque suspiciones miraque interpretationes in vilibus animis non producet?
units.tr: Indeed, since from the varied tempering of exhalations a contagion can arise in the air, which brings pestilence and death to men and cattle, and sterility, and harms the crops and trees, what harm will he not inflict on the human race once this has been stirred up? And since at a time of such plague the aforesaid meteors can naturally be more frequent, and will-o'-the-wisps cling about graves, because from these there is a greater supply of exhalations from those extinguished by plague, he gathers several of these into one, and gives cause to base souls to imagine spirits returning from the grave and announcing a greater pestilence, and to invent I know not what else. And if perhaps at this time a comet shines in the heavens, which the common people firmly persuade themselves is a most certain sign of impending war, pestilence, famine, and sterility, what cares and anxieties, what suspicions and marvellous interpretations will it not produce in base minds?

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Et ut magis nobis persuadeamus, quod etiam colorem varium iis omnibus suis ludibriis & terriculis inducere possit, cogitemus non solum quod siccuti ex diversis mixturis liquorum (uti vel ipsa pix liquida aquæ affusa, aut aqua sapone impregnata & in bullas inflata docet) varii colores oriuntur, ita etiam ab exhalationem diversitate; sed præsertim quod idem fiat ex simplici corporum versus radios varia positione, (uti in collo columbino &c. videre est) atque ex hac etiam iridis tam naturalis quàm artificialis jucunda repræsentatio, nubium colores varii: halonum & coronidum circa sidera apparentiæ &c. dependeant. Nam cum accuratissimè hæc omnia pictor hic excellentissimus perspecta habeat, cur non mixtis miscendis, contemperatis contemperandis, radiisque solaribus aut lunaribus debito modo objectis, omnium corporum species cum suis coloribus vivis repraesentare posset, atque ita aut tanquam juvenem talem pulchrum, prout angelos bonos depingunt, se exhibere; aut principem, prophetam, militem, monachum, puellam, serpentem, avem, feram rariffimam, & aliquando summe morstrosam; imo integras choreas, exercitus; Et similia infinita?
units.tr: And so that we may be more persuaded that he can also induce a varied colour with all these mockeries and terrors, let us consider not only that just as various colours arise from diverse mixtures of liquids (as even liquid pitch poured into water, or water impregnated with soap and blown into bubbles, shows), so too they arise from a diversity of exhalations; but especially that the same thing happens from the simple varied position of bodies with respect to the rays (as may be seen in the neck of a dove, etc.), and that from this also depend the pleasing representation of the rainbow, both natural and artificial, the various colours of clouds, and the appearances of halos and coronas around the stars, etc. For since this most excellent painter has all these things perceived most accurately, why could he not, by mixing what is to be mixed and tempering what is to be tempered, and by directing solar or lunar rays in the due manner, represent the forms of all bodies with their living colours, and thus present himself either as a beautiful young man, just as they paint good angels, or as a prince, a prophet, a soldier, a monk, a girl, a serpent, a bird, a very rare beast, and sometimes a most monstrous one; indeed whole dances and armies; and countless similar things?

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Novit non minus, qui aer nimis agitatus valde incalescat & ineptus reddatur, ad multorum animalium ignem vitalem confervandum, sed aptus ad extinguendum, unde suffocativus dicitur. Novit qui condensatus ad instar durissimi marmoris resistat, & subito rarefactus & a priore constrictione liberatus durissima quoque & gravissima propellat, frangat, comminuat, discutiat. Novit sonum nil aliud quam tremulum aeris motum esse, & quomodo in aere varii odores propagantur &c: Hinc pro lubitu suo aeri omnes has varietates inducens, nova alia producit. Sic v. gr. aere suffocante producto, equos ad anhelitus difficiles, spumae ex ore rejectionem, calcitrationem, variam jactationem incitat; aut odores, equae lascivientis similes objiciendo ad Venerem, & cursum indomitum, Et canibus odores ferarum, aut heri fui similes, aut illorum voces objiciendo, illos seducit. Sic condensato fortiter aëre brutis & peregrinantibus resistere ita potest, ut progredi non possint, etsi nil videant, quod obstet. Eodem modo corpora gravissima in libero aëre sustentare & sufferre potest, quo rarefacto iterum subito decidunt, & magno impetu cadendo substrata comminuunt; quo pacto & lapides, globos &c : tanquam ex funda, sclopetis &c : projicere potest. Nec quid obstat, quòd eodem in formam manûs, mallei, gladii &c : præcisé condensato & in corpora bestiarum hominumve fortiter impacto alapam infligat, quæ vestigium 5. digitorum, aut vulnus, quod vestigium mallei, gladii &c: referat, sic tamen ut nil, quod feriat, videatur.
units.tr: He knows no less how air, when too violently agitated, grows very hot and becomes unfit for keeping alive the vital fire of many animals, but apt for extinguishing it, whence it is called suffocating. He knows how air, when condensed, resists like the hardest marble, and when suddenly rarefied and freed from its previous compression, drives, breaks, crushes and shatters even the hardest and heaviest things. He knows that sound is nothing other than a tremulous motion of the air, and how various odours are propagated through the air, etc. Hence, by inducing all these varieties in the air at his pleasure, he produces other new things. Thus, for example, by producing a suffocating air, he stirs horses to difficult breathing, the expulsion of foam from the mouth, kicking, and various thrashing; or by presenting odours like those of a lascivious mare, he entices them to lust and unbridled running; and to dogs he presents the odours of wild beasts, or those like that of yesterday, or their voices, and so leads them astray. Likewise, by condensing the air strongly, he can so resist beasts and travellers that they cannot advance, even though they see nothing that stands in the way. In the same way he can hold up and bear heavy bodies in the open air, which, when the air is suddenly rarefied again, fall down, and in falling with great force crush whatever lies beneath; by which means he can also throw stones, balls, etc., as if from a sling or from muskets. Nor is there anything to prevent him, by condensing the air precisely into the form of a hand, a hammer, a sword, etc., and striking it forcefully against the bodies of beasts or men, from inflicting a slap which leaves the mark of five fingers, or a wound which resembles the mark of a hammer, a sword, etc., and yet nothing is seen that strikes.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Denique, quia ipsi satis perspectum est, quo pacto materia ignis aliaque cælorum (de quibus C. 3. § 1. 2. 3. Exc: 1.) fit causa omnis caloris, fermentationis, liquorum purificationis & (si ita loqui liceat) pellucidationis; gravitatis, luminis &c: ex quibus porrò mineralium, fossilium, plantarum, arborum, ipsorumque animalium generatio, imò omnia quæ, tam in terræ viscribus, quàm supra eam oriuntur intercuntque, dependent, quid mirum, si hisce suis aptissimis instrumentis utens non solùm herbas, plantas, arbores &c: multis modis alterare, sed eas etiam producere possit, uti & gemmas, metalla &c: & simulacra quædam ex hisce conflata: imò etiam mures, glires, aves &c: & uno nomine, res quasvis antea nunquam visas, & quarum simile quid forsan in rerum natura nondum extitit? Hæc igitur cùm ejus fiant opera, quorum quædam se ut automata habent, illa varié non tantum movere, sed etiam per illa loqui poterit, vel quatenus organis eorum ad vocem articulatam edendam aptis utitur; vel saltem aërem circa illa, modo illo, quo ad hæc aut illa verba significanda moveri debet concutiat; sic ut si os illorum suorum animalium, quis moveri videret, & simul hæc verba audiret, Diabolum per illa loquutum esse diceret. Quamvis hic motus oris non necessariò adsit, cùm & per statuas & simulacra loqui possit, & quidem jam hoc momento per hanc, altero per aliam; jam tanquam eminus, jam cominus; idque vel ad dextram, sinistram, sursum, deorsum &c:
units.tr: Finally, since it is quite well known to him how the matter of fire and the other heavenly bodies (concerning which see chap. 3, §§ 1, 2, 3, Exc. 1) becomes the cause of all heat, fermentation, purification of liquids and, if I may so speak, their clarification; of weight, of light, etc.; on which in turn depend the generation of minerals, fossils, plants, trees, and animals themselves, indeed all things that arise and perish both in the bowels of the earth and above it, what wonder if, using these most suitable instruments, he is able not only to alter herbs, plants, trees, etc. in many ways, but also to produce them, as well as gems, metals, etc., and certain images compounded from these; indeed even mice, dormice, birds, etc., and, in a word, any things never seen before, of which perhaps something similar has not yet existed in nature? Therefore, since these are his works, some of which are as automata, he will be able to move these variously, and also to speak through them, either insofar as he uses their organs, suited to uttering articulate speech, or at least by shaking the air around them in the manner in which it must be moved to signify these or those words; so that if someone should see the mouth of those creatures moving and at the same time hear these words, he would say that the Devil was speaking through them. Although this motion of the mouth is not necessarily present, since he can speak both through statues and images, and indeed at this moment through one, at the next through another; now as if from afar, now close at hand; and that either to the right, the left, upwards, downwards, etc.

units.la: &c: Hoc enim ex hoc solo mihi dependere videtur, quòd ab hac aut illa parte tremulus ille aëris motus, qui sonum vel vocem repræsentat, primò ab ipso directus sit. Sed quia infinita similia, quæ huc spectant explicare ex dictis possemus, quæ charta non caperet, paucis his contenti simus.
units.tr: etc. For this seems to depend on this alone, that the tremulous motion of the air, which represents sound or voice, is first directed by him from this or that side. But since we could explain from what has been said infinite similar things pertaining to this, which a page would not hold, let us be content with these few points.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: De Anglorum malorum in corpora Humana potentia.
units.tr: On the power of the evil angels over human bodies.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: QUandoquidem jam novimus, quot diversis instrumentis & modis agendi malus Genius instructus fit, quibus valet latè suum Imperium per aërem & terram exercere, multò facilius patebit ex Medicina quomodo his mediantibus in corpora nostra vim suam exerere valeat. Novit enim hic malus Genius multò distinctiùs quàm omnes Hippocrates & Galeni, quid subtilissima quævis materia in aërc existens, & totum nostrum corpus continuò pervadens, quid aër reliquus crassior illud circumfluens ; quid alimenta & medicamenta ab illo assumpta, & in succum & sanguinem conversa, possint boni malive præstare, & vel sanitatem vel innumeros morbos producere.
units.tr: Since we already know with what diverse instruments and modes of acting the evil Genius is equipped, by which he is able to exercise his dominion widely through air and earth, it will be made much more plain from medicine how, by these means, he is able to exert his power upon our bodies. For this evil Genius knows far more distinctly than all the Hippocrates and Galens what the most subtle matter existing in the air, continually pervading our whole body, and what the remaining, grosser air flowing around it can do for good or ill, and what foods and medicines taken in by it, once converted into juice and blood, can bring about, producing either health or countless diseases.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Horum aliquot exempla jam cap. præced. incidenter attigimus, sed ut magis hoc patescat specialiora quædam distinctius explicemus. Sic non tantum aëre calefacto & suffocativo reddito brutis hominibusque respirationem impedit, verum etiam vitam eripiet. Et hoc facillimo negotio in fossoribus qui in profundis terræ cavernis operantur impetrabit, quia ibidem subtilissimarum exhalationum maxima copia est, quæ ad sanguinis refrigerium, quod ad confervandum ignis vitalis vigorem summe necessarium est, ineptæ existunt & plerumque nimis crodentes sunt, qua propter per se valent vitam hominibus illis adimere, licèt non tam cito, quàm cùm à malo Genio copiosius & celerius agitatæ & versus eorum nares instar venti subtilissimi propulsæ, sanguinem impetuose & magnâ copiâ intrant. Sic vice versa aërem hominibus imminentem condensare & premere novit, ut illo gravati vix spiritum ducere, imo se ne quidem commovere valeant, quapropter humeris, collo vel capiti molem quandam impositam esse, aut aliquem inlidere, dicunt. Et quamvis non repugnet, illis molem aliquam à malo genio formatam, vel aliunde mediante aëre allatam revera imponi posse, attamen frequentius hoc ob morbum, qui incubus vocatur, fieri judico.
units.tr: We have touched incidentally on some examples of these in the preceding chapter, but to make this clearer we shall explain some of them more particularly and distinctly. Thus, when the air has been heated and made suffocating, he not only impedes breathing in beasts and men, but also takes away their life. And he will accomplish this with the greatest ease in miners who work in the deep caverns of the earth, because there is a very great abundance of the most subtle exhalations, which are unfit for the cooling of the blood (which is most necessary for preserving the vigour of the vital fire) and for the most part are excessively corrosive; for this reason they are of themselves able to take life away from those men, although not so quickly as when they are stirred up more copiously and rapidly by the evil Genius, driven towards their nostrils like the most subtle wind, and enter the blood violently and in great quantity. Likewise, conversely, he knows how to condense and press down the air hanging over men, so that, weighed down by it, they can scarcely draw breath, nay, can not even move; for this reason people say that some burden is placed on their shoulders, neck or head, or that someone presses upon them. And although it is not inconsistent that some mass formed by the evil genius, or brought in from elsewhere through the medium of the air, may really be placed upon them, nevertheless I judge that this more often happens on account of the disease which is called incubus.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: De contagio in aëre excitato, qui pestem &c. producere queat, Cap. præced. dictum. Eodem modo, si quid corrosivum & exedens ab exhalationibus secernat, & faciei cutique hominum applicet, illam denigrare, rubefacere, aut variis maculis, punctulatim dispersis deturpare; pustulas varias, scabiei, psoræ & lepræ, species inducere potest. Eædem particulæ cum aëre in pulmones ruentes ulcus & consequenter phtisin inducere, ad sanguinem vero & cor delatæ fermentationem ejus immutare & febrim, tormina &c: producent; Imo pars earum multò subtilior sursum ad cerebrum tendens illud perturbare, & vel vertiginem, qua omnia in gyrum circumrotari videntur, vel aliam quandam noxam cerebro inferre; indeque ad musculos & nervosum genus omne ipsumque sanguinem delata, novas turbas dare poterit.
units.tr: Concerning the contagion excited in the air, which can produce plague etc., mentioned in the preceding chapter: in the same way, if he separates out something corrosive and eating away from the exhalations and applies it to the face and skin of men, he can blacken it, redden it, or disfigure it with various spots scattered like dots; he can induce various pustules, and kinds of scabies, psora and leprosy. The same particles, rushing with the air into the lungs, can induce ulcer and consequently phthisis, and when carried to the blood and heart they can alter its fermentation and produce fever, gripings and so on; indeed, a part of them, much more subtle, tending upward to the brain, can disturb it, either bringing on vertigo, by which all things seem to whirl round in a circle, or inflicting some other harm upon the brain; and from there, carried down to the muscles and the whole nervous kind and the blood itself, it will be able to cause new disorders.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Quomodo diversimodè in oculos per sua repræsentamina ; in aures per alloquutiones ; in nares per odores , maximé tetricos, & sine quibus post se reliĉis non recedere dicitur ; in linguam per diversos sapores agere , & sic lumine vel sono fortissimo ; odoribus pessimis & saporibus erodentibus organa hæc sensuum , imò totum corpus,totumque hominem lædere possit ex cap. præced. satis constabit. At referunt etiam speĉtra alia calida, vel frigida; alia humida, vel sicca apparuisse ; imò malum Genium cum sagis aĉtum Venereum, exercuisse , & similia, quæ sensuum taĉtus magis concernunt. Unde hæc? Concipi equidem facilè potest , quòd , si corpus a Diabolo formatum multis exhalationibus oleosis & sulphureis constet, flammamque aliquam levem concipiat exteriorem ejus superficiem solùm depascentem , hocque corpus applicetur protinus homini, calorem sit exhibiturum, imò qui aliquando urat ; sed si non statim applicetur, sic ut per flammam materia combustibilis prius sit consumta, aliâ crassiore relictâ ; aut si solùm hoc corpus sit lucidum & non ardens , frigidum apparebit. Uno verbo , quò corporum talium minima naturalia erunt magis agitata, eo plus calida; quo minus, eo plus frigida; quo plus liquoris in se habebunt eo magis humida; quo minus eo magis sicca erunt. Sed quantum ad sagas; etsi non implicet Diabolum corpore hunc in finem effecto titillationem venereams inferre, & quia ipsi jus in corpus suum sagae concesserunt impraegnationis speciem, ipsarum sanguine, vel solo nutu voluntatis alterato, suscitare posse, unde ranas, bufones, aliave infecta sagae enituntur; attamen judico id potius in deceptione & illusione continua consistere, de qua inferius. Nam generaliter bene notari velim, quod illa omnia phaenomena, quae Diabolus sensibus externis hominum objicit, raro tam perfecta sint, uti de eis homines loquuntur; sed quod imaginatio, meticulositas, & praecipue mendax fama, quae semper crescit eundo, formam eis det exactam & elaboratam magis, quam unquam in rei veritate fuit; uti itidem hoc ex infra dicendis confirmabitur.
units.tr: How he can injure the eyes in various ways through his appearances, the ears through speeches, and the nose through odours, especially foul ones, without which he is said not to depart when left behind; how he can act on the tongue through different tastes, and so, by very strong light or sound, by the worst odours and corrosive tastes, injure these organs of the senses, indeed the whole body and the whole man, will be sufficiently clear from the preceding chapter. But they also report that other apparitions have appeared, some warm or cold, others moist or dry; indeed that an evil Genius has performed the venereal act with witches, and similar things, which concern the sense of touch more. Whence do these things come? It can indeed easily be conceived that if a body formed by the Devil consists of many oily and sulphurous exhalations, and conceives some light flame that consumes only its outer surface, and this body is applied at once to a man, it will exhibit heat, and sometimes even burn him; but if it is not applied at once, so that the combustible matter is first consumed by the flame and a thicker residue is left, or if this body is only luminous and not burning, it will appear cold. In a word, the more the minute natural particles of such bodies are agitated, the warmer they are; the less agitated, the colder; the more liquid they hold within themselves, the moister; the less, the drier. But as to witches: although it does not involve the Devil, having made a body for this purpose, in bringing a venereal titillation, and although the witches have granted him right over their bodies, he can stir up a kind of impregnation by altering their blood or by the mere nod of his will, whence witches bring forth frogs, toads and other unclean things; yet I judge that this consists rather in deception and continual illusion, of which more below. For in general I would have it well noted that all those phenomena which the Devil presents to men's external senses are rarely as perfect as men describe them; rather, imagination, timidity and especially lying report, which always grows as it goes, gives them a form more exact and elaborated than they ever had in the truth of the matter; as will also be confirmed from what is said below.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Prae aliis autem hic consideration em meretur, quomodo per illa, quae affumuntur & in succum & sanguinem convertuntur, malitiam suam exercere valeat. Nam etsi homicida hic omnium maximus animis hominum praecipue inhiet, [illegible, ~3 letters]iet, attamen vitam quoque illorum aut saltem valetudinem, si prius ipsi non licet, perdere tentat. Novit enim, quòd corpore male disposito mens in confortium trahatur, doloribusque & molestiis vexata ad suas proprias actiones at-què ac ad illas quæ à conjugio mentis corporisque dependent, inepta facilè reddatur. Novit etiam non solùm, quòd temperamenta corporis sequantur mores animi, sed etiam exactissimam omnium temperamentorum cognitionem habet, & quomodo in mentem agant, quæque ad suæ voluntati optemderandum magis idonea sint; hinc saltem ut ea quæ minus apta sunt per morbos aliaque media mutet nunquam non invigilat.
units.tr: Among other things, however, this deserves consideration here: how he may be able to exercise his malice through the things that are taken in and converted into juice and blood. For although this greatest of all murderers chiefly thirsts after men's souls, yet he also tries to destroy their life, or at least their health, if he is not permitted the former. For he knows that when the body is ill-disposed the mind is drawn into fellowship with it, and, vexed by pains and troubles, is easily rendered unfit for its own proper actions, and for those which depend on the union of mind and body. He knows also not only that the temperaments of the body follow the dispositions of the mind, but he has the most exact knowledge of all temperaments, and of how they act upon the mind, and which are most suitable for bending to his will; hence he never ceases to watch how he may change, through diseases and other means, those that are less apt.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Totum igitur corpus quia præcipuè perdere & destruere allaborat, hunc in finem quo potest modo alimenta corrumpit, vel ut loquuntur veneno inficit. Hoc quomodo mediantibus illis, quæ sub forma cibi & potûs assumuntur impetret, ultimò jam paucis inquirendum. Et sanè hoc ipsi facile est. 1: Quia novit multò melius quàm ullus Botanicus & Chymicus naturam omnium herbarum, mineralium &c cùm ipse (ut dictum §.9. C. præc.) variasherbas, varia minera-lia. Iia producere quicat, ideòque ipsi facile sit tale quid producere, quod respectu hujus aut illius temperamenti venenum est, & adhuc facilius, ea venena quæ jam existunt cognoscere. 2: Cumque illa subtilissimarum partium esse queant, ut, separatim in aëre illis particulis existentibus, nullo modo percipiantur, (uti contagium pestis &c: ) nullo animadvertente, cibo potuique illas miscere, idque citissime poterit. Cùmque hæ particulæ se ut fermenta subtilissima & efficaciffima respectu corporis hujus aut illius hominis habeant, pro diversa illarum qualitate & attemperatione, cùm ventriculi fermento naturali mixtæ erunt, vel solùm nauseam, vel vomitum simul, tormina, & inflatio nem &c. producent. Et hæc medicamentis etiam hominibus cognitis facilè conficiet. At forsan non iisdem 3. vermes varii generis; uti & insecta, quorum aliqua tam perfecta sunt, ut sonitum diversorum animalium, v.gr. ranarum, pipionum, murium &c: referant, quæ alias procreare didicit. Quod sanè mirum adeò non est, cùm Chymici ex certis mifturis, fimi equini calore fovente, aliisque modis, infecta varia producere nôrint; At certè fimi equini calore, multo aptior esse poterit ad hunc effectum impetrandum digestio illa, quæ in ventriculo perficitur. Multò minus 4. mirum, quod talia fermenta cibis potuique miscere sciat, quæ post levem aliquam in ventriculo ebullitionem cum partibus cibi variis modis conjunguntur & concrescunt, atque ita calcem, arenam, cretam, lapillos, scobem ferri,&c. imitentur, uti ex oleo tartari & vitrioli mixto, corpus albicans & durum, quod tartarum vitriolatum nominamus, per fermentationem subitanceam oriri videmus. Aut 5. si lentior fit illa fermentatio, cum certis ciborum particulis junctis, & secundum longitudinem extensis speciem capillorum, filorum &c: rudimenta futurorum vermium existentium, referent. Uti constat vermes in ventriculo & intestinis natos ex innumera congerie talium filamentorum, diversos etiam colores habentium, quasi conflatos esse: Magis 6. mirandum quomodo aciculas, & ferramenta minora sæpius dicantur veneficio infectos ejicere, quia, nisi cibo & potui à malo Genio ejusque servis sint mixta, non ita liquet quomodo ad instar priorum in ventriculo generari queant. Quamvis putem me experimentum aliquod Chymicum legisse, ad cujus ideam hoc aliquomodo explicari posset. At 7. fidem fere superat, & à me nondum bcne concipi posse fateor, quòd referant integros cultros, serras, magnos clavos, magna frusta panni &c: à veneficio infectis evomi; de quibus idcirco nihil jam determino, nisi quòd potiùs ad illusiones & meras apparentias à Diabolo effictas, & quòd unum pro alio corpore substituere queat, referam.
units.tr: Since he labours above all to ruin and destroy the whole body, he corrupts the food to this end in whatever way he can, or, as they say, infects it with poison. How he may bring this about through those things which are taken in as food and drink must now finally be enquired into briefly. And indeed this is easy for him. (1) Because he knows the nature of all herbs, minerals and so on far better than any botanist or chemist, since he himself (as said in §9 of the preceding chapter) can produce various herbs and various minerals, it is easy for him to produce something which is poison with respect to this or that temperament, and even easier to recognise the poisons that already exist. (2) And since these can consist of the most subtle particles, so that, existing separately in the air, they are in no way perceived (as with the contagion of plague and so on), he can mix them with food and drink without anyone noticing, and that very quickly. And since these particles stand towards the body of this or that man as the most subtle and most efficacious ferments, according to their different quality and temperament, when mixed with the stomach's natural ferment they will produce either only nausea, or vomiting together with cramps, inflation and so on. And this he can easily accomplish with medicaments known even to men. But perhaps not with the same ease (3) various kinds of worms, and also insects, some of which are so perfect that they imitate the sounds of various animals, e.g. frogs, pigeons, mice and so on, which he has learned to produce in other ways. This is indeed not so wonderful, since chemists know how to produce various insects from certain mixtures, with the warmth of horse dung fostering them, and by other means; but certainly the digestion carried out in the stomach can be far more apt for bringing about this effect than the warmth of horse dung. Much less (4) is it wonderful that he knows how to mix with food and drink such ferments which, after a slight boiling in the stomach, combine and coagulate in various ways with the parts of the food, and so imitate lime, sand, chalk, little stones, iron filings and so on; just as we see a white and hard body, which we call vitriolated tartar, arise from a mixture of oil of tartar and vitriol through a sudden fermentation. Or (5) if that fermentation is slower, with certain particles of food joined together and extended lengthwise, they may resemble the rudiments of future worms; for it is established that worms born in the stomach and intestines are, as it were, compounded from an innumerable heap of such filaments, which also have various colours. More (6) to be wondered at is how needles and smaller iron tools are often said to be ejected by those infected with witchcraft, since, unless they have been mixed with food and drink by the evil Genius and his servants, it is not clear how they could be generated in the stomach like the former. Although I think I have read of some chemical experiment by whose idea this might in some way be explained. But (7) it almost exceeds belief, and I confess I cannot yet well conceive, that they report whole knives, saws, large nails and large pieces of cloth being vomited by those infected with poison; concerning these therefore I determine nothing for now, except that I would rather refer them to illusions and mere appearances fashioned by the Devil, and to his being able to substitute one body for another.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: His igitur & multis aliis modis ventriculi fermento ex naturali statu planè deturbato, quid mirum si inde totius sanguinis bona constitutio perdatur, sic ut ita diabolus consequenter termina, rugitus, murmura, rugitus varios; ventris insufflationem immanem: dolores capitis & deliria horrenda: mictum sanguinis aut hæmorrhagiam narium maximam; ulcera fœda & maculas turpissimas; febrem lentam & tabem consummatissimam; & verbo, nullos non cruciatus & morbos quibus corpora hominum tentari possunt causet.
units.tr: Given these and many other ways in which the ferment of the stomach is entirely thrown out of its natural state, what wonder is it if the good constitution of the whole blood is then lost? In this way the devil, as a consequence, causes gripings, groanings, murmurs, various rumblings, huge inflation of the belly, horrible headaches and delirium, the passing of blood in the urine or a very great nosebleed, foul ulcers and most shameful spots, a slow fever and the most complete wasting, and, in a word, every kind of torment and disease with which human bodies can be assailed.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Si tamen ipsi non liceat effectus tales votis suis planè respondentes hisce mediis obtinere, Deo hæc opera Diaboli destruente, aut ne omnem effectum fortiantur impedionte, sæpius tamen hæc fermenta, aliquas saltem suarum viribus exerentia, ad temperamenta hominum.
units.tr: Yet if it is not permitted to him to obtain effects that fully match his wishes by these means, either because God destroys the devil's works or because something impedes the full effect, nonetheless these ferments, exerting at least some of their powers, will often alter the temperaments of men.

units.la: {y} Hæc tamen intra sapientiam ... num mutanda sufficiunt, sicuti notum est chymicis, quomodo idem corpus vel solo gradu caloris paucissimisque aliis mutatis, aliam naturam induat; sic ut ex eadem materia vomitorium, purgans, sudoriferum, alterans, imò corroborans fieri queat. Quocunque a. modo se temperamenta habeant, sive naturaliter talia sint, aut naturali morbo mutata; aut cooperante Diabolo; paucis exemplis quid per illa sola in corpus & consequenter in animam producat, jam videamus.
units.tr: These things, however, are enough to show that the temperaments can be changed, as is known to chemists: how the same body, by a change of heat alone and very few other changes, takes on a different nature, so that from the same material an emetic, a purgative, a sudorific, an alterative, or even a restorative can be made. Whatever way the temperaments may be, whether they are naturally such or changed by a natural disease, or with the devil cooperating, let us now see, by a few examples, what they produce in the body and consequently in the soul through these alone.

units.la: CAP. III. De malorum Angelorum in Corpo- ra hominum potentia per solum temperamentum.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. On the power of evil angels over the bodies of men, through the temperament alone.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: HActenus qua ratione Diabolus mundo majore ad minorem perdendum utatur vidimus, restat ut consideremus, quomodo ipsius corporis viribus ad nocendum homini, quoad corpus quidem directe, consequenter vero quoad mentem ejus utatur. Vires igitur ejus eam in temperamento suo naturali consistant, inter illud occurrit primò quod sanguineum dicitur. Hoc autem cum præ aliis temperatissimum sit, & corpus validum & vegetum faciat, non ita directè ad noxam aliquam ipsi inferendam Diabolo inservit, sed solùm indirectè. V. gr. quia hoc temperamentum homines ad Venerem instigat, Diabolus factam hanc de objecto Venereo impressionem in cerebro, facilè tam fortem & distinctam facere potest, mittendo similes spiritus animales versus eandem partem cerebri, ut inflammatus quasi œstro Venereo ejusmodi, rejecto omni pudore & usu rationis ad lasciviam, scortationes, & adulteria laxatis quasi habenis ruat, quo sicuti mentem suam & famam deturpat, sic corpus enervat.
units.tr: So far we have seen by what method the devil uses the greater world to destroy the lesser. It remains to consider how he uses the powers of the body itself to harm man, directly as to the body and consequently as to the mind. His powers lie in the natural temperament, and the first of these to present itself is the one called sanguine. Since this is more temperate than the others and makes the body strong and vigorous, it does not serve the devil directly to inflict any harm, but only indirectly. For example, since this temperament urges men toward Venus, the devil can easily make the impression of the Venereal object on the brain very strong and distinct, by sending similar animal spirits toward the same part of the brain. The man, inflamed as if by a Venereal gadfly, casts off all shame and use of reason and rushes, reins loosed, into lust, fornication and adultery. By this he disfigures his mind and reputation, and so weakens his body.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: At multò magis ipsius intentione aptum est illud quod valde biliosum est, quia illi homines naturaliter ad iram, odium, invidiamque tam proclives sunt, ut horum vitiorum signa ipsis oculorum actionibus, frontis plicis, faciei rubore vel pallore, &c : ob levissimam quoque ansam offendant ; vitia sane quæ cum natura Diaboli à nobis Exc. priore descripta præ cæteris conveniunt, sic ut in illis suam imaginem quasi videat, & ob id de meliore suæ intentionis successu spesperct. Hinc sicuti illis ita novit uti, ut indirecte hominibus talibus noceat, dum hæc vitia matres quasi rixarum; vulnerum & homicidii sunt, propter quæ homines famæ, fortunæ, corporis & vitæ, imo sæpius mentis & salutis æternæ jactuiam patiuntur, sic directe temperamentum hoc usurpat ad excitandas febres ardentes & quæ inde fluunt deliria, memoriæ imbecillitas &c: passiones colicas; diarrhæas fortissimas & dysenterias, & similes morbos, quibus homines talis temperamenti naturaliter obnoxios esse Medicis notum est.
units.tr: But the bilious temperament is far more suited to his purpose, because men of this kind are so naturally prone to anger, hatred and envy that they betray these vices by the movements of their eyes, the wrinkles of the brow, the redness or paleness of the face, and so on, and take offence at the slightest occasion. These are the vices which agree best with the nature of the devil described by us in the earlier Exercitation, so that he sees, as it were, his own image in them and hopes for better success for his purpose because of them. Hence, just as he knows how to use these vices to harm such men indirectly, since they are, as it were, the mothers of quarrels, wounds and murder, on account of which men suffer loss of reputation, fortune, body and life, and very often even of mind and eternal salvation, so he uses this temperament directly to excite burning fevers and the delirium that flows from them, weakness of memory, and so on; colic pains, very violent diarrhoeas and dysenteries, and similar diseases, to which, as physicians know, men of this temperament are naturally liable.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Præ aliis tamen ipsi maximè commodum est temperamentum valde melancholicum, & à quo pituitosum parum discrepat. Hoc equidem nomine etiam, quòd morbos qui indè propulsare possunt, facillimo negotio producat, foveat, augeatque, maximè tamen ob id quòd tales homines naturaliter ad tristitiam inclinent; solitudinem ament; atque in consideratione hujus aut illius objecti, præsertim tristis, diu & mordicus quasi hæreant; meticulosi etiam sint & ob minima alterentur, consternanturque, plerumque vilissimi, tam quoad mentem, quàm quoad corpus exiitant. In illis enim aptissimum quasi
units.tr: Yet the most convenient of all for him is the very melancholic temperament, which differs little from the phlegmatic. He produces, fosters and increases the diseases that can arise from it with the greatest ease. This is partly so for the same reason, but chiefly because such men are naturally inclined to sadness, love solitude, and cling long and tenaciously, as it were, to the contemplation of this or that object, especially a sad one. They are also timid, and are disturbed and dismayed by the smallest things, and for the most part they turn out very base, both in mind and in body. For in them he finds, as it were, a most suitable stage on which to play his own part, that of the spirit of pride, the deceiver, the liar and the murderer.

units.la: theatrum invenit, in quo suam personam, hoc est, spiritum superbiæ, decep-torem, mendacem & homicidam agit. Nam cùm ipsi nullum gaudium quasi majus evenire possit, quàm si homines ad desperationem deducat, ut sibi, de salute æterna desperantes, & à Christo ad hostem ejus Diabolum deficientes, violentas manus ipsis inferant; idque tam grande facinus sit, quo ipso vix dignius quid patrare potest, ideòque nec uno insultu, sed tractu temporis & per occultas insidias & artes, quibus animo & corpore fortes melius resistere possunt, in hominibus talibus melancholicis, uti eos descripsimus, citius se exop-tatum eventum assequi posse, apprime novit.
units.tr: For no greater joy can befall him than to lead men into despair, so that, despairing of their eternal salvation and falling away from Christ to his enemy the devil, they lay violent hands on themselves. Since so great a crime is one he can scarcely accomplish more worthily, he knows full well that he can reach the desired outcome in melancholic men of the kind we have described. He does this not by a single assault but over time, through secret snares and arts, against which the strong in mind and body can better resist.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Gradus igitur aliquos, per quos in expugnando tali homine progreditur distinctius consideremus. Et 1. quidem in eo consistere potest, quòd conservans eundem motum spirituum, quo sibi homo, maximè in solitudine, quæ aptior est ad profundiorem contemplationem, aliquod objectum, & præsertim quod tristitiæ causa est, repræsentat, passionem præsentem firmat, adauget; unde objectum quod considerat, tandem imaginationi ejus tam vividum exhi-bebitbebitur, ut sicuti in imaginatione illeʿ est, ita etiam extra suum corpus existerejudicet ; Non aliter, ut qui ociosè nubes & ignem &c : defixis oculis contemplatur, varia in ipsis corpora oriri & interire quasi videbit, quorum imagines tamen solum modò in ejus forti imaginatione subsistunt. Sed quia hæc apparentia quam extra fe melancholicus esse revera putat, statim disparet, quia metus, vel terror, vel alia quædam passio superveniens, cursum hunc spirituum animalium, qui ad fortem hanc imaginationem requirebatur mutat, hinc certò fe spectrum vidisse concludit. Cùm autem hoc melancholico sæpiùs evenire possit, hinc habitum quasi metus & confternationis contrahit. Hoc modo viduæ melancholicæ demortuus maritus, quem impensè amavit facilé reducitur ; amatoribus illa persona, quam vehementer amant, ostenditur ; avaro opes, quarum cupiditate flagrat & anxiè quæ- rit, monstratur &c :
units.tr: Let us therefore consider more distinctly some stages by which he advances in overcoming such a man. The first may consist in this: keeping the same flow of spirits in motion, by which the man, especially in solitude, which is better suited to deep contemplation, sets before himself some object, particularly one that is the cause of his sadness, and so confirms and increases the present passion. Hence the object he considers will at last be presented to his imagination so vividly that, just as it is in his imagination, he judges it to exist outside his body too. It is as with one who idly gazes with fixed eyes at clouds or fire: he will seem to see various bodies arising and perishing in them, whose images, however, subsist only in his strong imagination. But because this appearance, which the melancholic really thinks exists outside himself, immediately vanishes, since fear or terror or some other passion coming on changes the course of the animal spirits that this strong imagination required, he therefore concludes with certainty that he has seen a spectre. Since this can happen to the melancholic quite often, he contracts, as it were, a habit of fear and consternation. In this way the widow's dead husband, whom she loved intensely, is easily brought back to her; to lovers the person they passionately love is shown; to the miser the riches, for whose desire he burns and which he anxiously seeks, are displayed, etc.:

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: At II. quia melancholicus ad communem ferè omnium hominum morem (confer C. 3 §. 7. Exc I) Deum, mentem suam, mortem, tam naturalem quàm æternam, Diabolos, pœnas & gaudia æter- na non nisi sub imagine corporea repræfentat,hunc perversum conceptum Diabolus,modo jam dicto, figit, ut præconcepta & falsa opinio quæ inde nascitur, ex ejus animo difficillime exscindatur, & habitus perversus, jam ab infantia contractus magis perficiatur, sic ut tandem impossibile ipsi fiat de Deo & rebus intelligibilibus aliud quid quàm corporeum & fallum concipere. Nam ex hoc mens talis hominis non potest non quasi carnalis & animal quasi brutum fieri, quod nullo modo sapere poterit id quod est Spiritus Dei, sed quod ridiculum & stultum putat quid, de Deo &c: absque imagine apprehendere. Hinc a vero Dei cultu necessario declinans, & alium quam Deus non vult ex imaginatione sua fingens, spirituique Deo contradicens, nec ipsi se ubiciens, optatum quasi Diaboli diverticulum se exhibet, quo opportuno tempore utatur ut hominem per semetipsum vinciat, vincat, & quoad corpus & animam perdat.
units.tr: Second, because the melancholic, like nearly all people in common practice (see Chapter 3, §7, Exc. I), represents God, his own mind, death (both natural and eternal), the devils, and eternal punishments and joys only under a bodily image, the devil, by the means just mentioned, fixes this distorted conception in him. The result is that the preconceived and false opinion which arises from it is very hard to root out of his mind, and the perverse habit, already acquired from infancy, is further confirmed, so that in the end it becomes impossible for him to conceive of God and intelligible things as anything other than corporeal and false. For from this, the mind of such a man cannot but become, as it were, carnal and his soul, as it were, brutish. He will be unable to perceive in any way what is the Spirit of God, but takes it to be foolish and ridiculous to grasp God and other things without an image. Hence, necessarily turning aside from the true worship of God, and fashioning for himself, out of his imagination, something other than what God wills, and resisting the Spirit of God, and not submitting himself to him, he presents himself as a ready-made lodging for the devil, which the devil may use at the opportune time to ensnare the man by his own self, overcome him, and destroy him in body and soul.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Nam III. opportunitatem hanc Diabolus facile inveniet. Ita v. gr. vel hoc solo quod ejusmodi homo carnalis sibi mortem ut terribilium terribilissimum imaginetur, hanc ideam Diabolus confirmando ipsum ita terrere potest & simul mundo affigere, ut vel solum mortis nomen ipsum expavescere faciat, cujus considerationem ut tollat mundi delicias quæ rat. Hinc quia nîl horribiliùs &dolorificum magis, quàm mori censet, quæcunque ipsi de æternis gaudiis & cœlesti gloria, quibus nisi post mortem possumus indui, dicentur, nunquam tanti faciet, ut ob ea mori vellet; nam licèt libenter eis potiri vellet, non tamen per tam duram & asperrimam viam ( ut ipsi videtur ) ad illa transire cupit. Unde mavult temporalibus frui, quam ob æterna gaudia mori. Non aliquot pueri quidem sanitatem affectant, at potionem amaram cbibere nolunt, malintque valetudinarii manere & mori, quam sanitatem ingrato medio recipere
units.tr: Thirdly, the devil will easily find this opportunity. For example, from the very fact that such a carnal man imagines death as the most terrible of terrors, the devil, by confirming this idea, can so frighten him and at the same time fix him to the world that the mere name of death makes him tremble; to avoid thinking of it, he seeks the delights of the world. Hence, since he judges nothing more dreadful and painful than dying, whatever is said to him about eternal joys and heavenly glory (into which we can be clothed only after death) will never be valued so highly by him that he would wish to die for them. For although he would gladly possess them, he does not desire to pass to them by so hard and rough a way (as it seems to him). So he prefers to enjoy temporal things rather than die for eternal joys. Some children, indeed, do desire health, yet they refuse to drink a bitter potion, and would rather remain sickly and die than recover health by an unpleasant means. ## VII.

units.la: VII.

Quousque jam homine tali irretito si IV. eveniat ut damna aliqua ingentia fortunæ, famæ, corporisve patiatur; Ut si ad paupertatem redigatur, si injuriis gravetur, si cruciatibus & morbis tenea- tur, tunc demum suam Diabolus imaginem, & cruciatus infernales quales sibi talis homo fingere solet, in memoriam revocat. Sed multò horribiliorem, sic ut mortis imago præ his pulcrafit; simul hæc sua damna ut justam pœnam Dei, quâ ob peccata hæc & illa, innu-
units.tr: When such a man is thus ensnared, and thirdly it happens that he suffers some great losses of fortune, reputation or body, for instance if he is reduced to poverty, if he is wronged, if he is racked by torments and diseases, then at last the devil recalls to his memory his own image and the infernal torments which such a man is accustomed to imagine for himself. But he presents them far more horrible, so that the image of death seems a trifle beside them. At the same time he sets these losses before him as the just punishment of God, by which innumerable and very great punishments are inflicted for these and those sins, and which, though it is still the least of the punishments about to come, is so great that he cannot be equal to bearing them all.

units.la: īnnumera & maxima punitur, & quæ instantium pœnarum adhuc minima sit, objicit, sic ut omnibus illis ferendis par non possit esse. Hinc cruciatus & morsus conscientiæ quidem innumeri in tali animo surgunt, at non est tristitia secundum Deum, quem (juxta th. 5. hujus) nunquam agnovit, sed ejus loco Principem summé iratum, & implacabilem; ignem & flammam consumentem & simile quid imaginans, præ anxietate quò se vertat non habet, ubique quasi spectris illi occurrentibus, quæ interius imaginationi ejus Diabolus obtrudit. Inter tot mala & spectra ergo quasi versans, quorum quodlibet morte multò horribiliorem judicat, facilè suam sententiam mutat, & quia mortuos judicat nullos dolores ampliùs sentire, & quæ de vita alia post mortem sæpius audivit, esse nugas, nec futuram talem unquam resurrectionem &c: inter omnia mala hoc minimum esse concludit mori & finire morte dolores, & quidem subito, ut quasi mortem, seu terriculum illud crudele præveniat, ne ab illo diutius totqueatur. Et sic Diabolus tragœdiam suam finit.
units.tr: Hence indeed countless pangs and gnawings of conscience arise in such a mind, but it is not godly sorrow, since he has never known God (according to thesis 5 of this section), but in his place imagines a supremely angry and implacable Prince, a consuming fire and flame, and similar things. Overwhelmed with anxiety, he has no idea where to turn, since on every side there come upon him, as it were, phantoms which the devil thrusts inwardly into his imagination. Thus, turning amid so many evils and phantoms, each of which he judges far more horrible than death, he easily changes his opinion. And since he judges that the dead feel no pains any more, and has often heard that the talk of another life after death is nonsense, and that there will be no such resurrection, he concludes that among all evils this is the least: to die, and by death to end his pains, and that quickly, so that he may anticipate death, or that cruel terror, and not be tormented by it any longer. And so the devil ends his tragedy. ## VIII.

units.la: VIII.

Sed hîc bene notari velim; medum de melancholico hæc refero non tamen reliqua temperamenta excludere, Ioquor enim solùm jam de aptissimo; Quippe illa aptitudo uti in solo corpore consistit ita medicamentis, musica hilari, consortio læto &c: atque ita simul hic malus Genius potest pelli, id est, hæc aptitudo quam malus Genius ad nocendum homini invenit. Certum enim est quòd Diabolus idem in aliis quoque temperamentis obtinere possit, quamvis (si solùm corpus respicias) non tam facile. Hujusque rationem unam & sufficientissimam damus hanc: quod quemadmodum mens nostra ultimò per spiritus animales operarur in corpus suum, & per illos etiam patitur (juxta C. I. §. 8. Exc. I.) sic itidem & malus Genius in mentem humanam agat, ac ob id quoties spiritus animales eodem modo in ventriculis fluere & quasi radiare nutu suæ voluntatis faciat, quod requiritur ad hoc vel illud menti humanæ repræsentandum, toties ea perceptio in mente illa oriatur, qualis naturaliter ipsi evenire debet (juxta Exc. I. C. I §. 7.) Atque ita non solùm in insomniis illam terrere, & ut hæc vel illa quasi videat, audiat &c: efficit, sed de die quoque imaginationem hanc occupans, extra suum corpus hæc & illa audire, videre &c: efficiet; unde fascinationum variæ species emergunt.
units.tr: But I would have it carefully noted here: although I relate these things of the melancholic, I do not thereby exclude the other temperaments; I speak only of the most suitable one. For that suitability consists in the body alone, and so it can be driven out by medicines, cheerful music, joyful company and the like; and in this way that evil genius can be expelled, that is, this suitability which the evil genius has found for harming a man. For it is certain that the devil can obtain the same advantage over other temperaments as well, though (if you look at the body alone) not so easily. We give one sufficient reason for this: just as our mind ultimately acts upon its body through the animal spirits, and is in turn affected through them (according to chap. 1 §8, Exc. I), so too the evil genius acts upon the human mind. Accordingly, whenever he causes the animal spirits to flow in the ventricles in the same way, and to radiate, as it were, at the nod of his will, which is required for representing this or that to the human mind, that perception arises in that mind just as it ought naturally to arise for him (according to Exc. I, chap. 1 §7). And so he not only terrifies the mind in dreams, making it seem to see or hear this or that, but, occupying the imagination by day as well, he will make it hear and see things outside its own body. Hence various kinds of fascinations emerge.

units.la: Hinc enim aliis quæ videre volunt, ut furem, amasiam, &c: in circulo terræ inscripto: aliis in speculo, aliis in aëre &c: repræsentat; Perinde enim ipsi est ubi ea repræsentet, quia sufficit clara & distincta illa imaginatio interius menti humanæ objecta, ut judicet illa, quæ solùm in cerebro suo quasi videt, in locis illis, quæ oculo opposita sunt, existere. Unde manifeste patet non solùm infinita pro spectris extra hominem apparentibus haberi, quæ tamen non sunt, verùm etiam difficulter determinari posse, quando, quod ut spectrum appareret, revera fit aliquid à Diabolo in aëre formatum.
units.tr: For he presents to some the things they wish to see, such as a thief or a mistress, drawn in a circle on the ground; to others in a mirror, to others in the air, and so on. For it makes no difference to him where he presents them, since that clear and distinct imagination placed before the human mind is enough for it to judge that what it sees only in its brain exists in those places which lie opposite the eye. Hence it is plainly clear that not only are countless things taken for phantoms appearing outside a man, which in fact are not, but also that it can be hard to determine when something actually formed in the air by the devil is what appears as a phantom.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Tandem, ex dictis clarè patet, quomodo Genius malus morbis, facillimè uti possit ad homines terrendos, decipiendos cruciandosque. Sic quàm facilè fe deliriis febricitantium, & epilepsiæ variis symptomatibus, & fomnambulonum actionibus, immiscet? Atque, cum qui incubum patiuntur (morbum naturalem fcil:) ex vulgi superstitione putantes illum à nescio quo Genio lascivo induci, opinentur fe à lemuribus infestari & subigi, facilè illos in sua opinione confirmari, ut negleêtis ordinariis remediis ad superstitiosam curam consugiant, sed etiam aliquid de suo in tali morbo addit. Et cùm uterus sit infinitorum malorum mater, sitque sexus fœmineus temperamenti magis frigidi & aquosi seu melancholici, animamque viliorem habeat; multò magis illas Diaboli tentationibus obnoxias esse, quis non videt? Hinc non solùm picâ, furore uterino, epilepsiâ uterinâ præsente; &c: suam vim facilius exercet; & sua negotia ordinario naturæ cursui miscet, sed etiam multò rarius viros quàm fœminas, & inter illas vetulas & conditionis inferioris & male educatas irretire potest, ut sagarum more vel alio quocunque modo ipsi inserviant; imò tentatio illa omnium maxima & horribilissima quæ obsessio corporalis vocatur, rarius in viris quàm in fœminis invenitur; & illæ rursus eo magis huic obnoxiæ sunt, quæ furorem uterinum aliumve similem uteri affectum patiuntur. Quæcunque a. in tali obsessione observantur; aut in hominibus incarceratis, quibus collum obtortum à Diabolo esse dicitur; aut etiam aliis in aqua variè laceratis, aut similibus quæ huc spectant, ex eis quæ his Exercitationibus dicta sunt, posse satis probabiliter educi & probari judicamus.
units.tr: Finally, from what has been said it is clear how the evil Genius can very easily use diseases to terrify, deceive and torment human beings. How readily does he mingle himself with the delirium of the feverish, with the various symptoms of epilepsy, and with the actions of sleepwalkers? And since those who suffer from incubus (a natural disease, namely) think, through the superstition of the common people, that it is brought on by some lascivious Genius, they suppose themselves to be troubled and oppressed by specters. It is easy for the Genius to confirm them in this opinion, so that, neglecting ordinary remedies, they flee to superstitious cure, and he adds something of his own to such a disease. And since the womb is the mother of countless ills, and the female sex has a colder and watery or melancholic temperament and a baser soul, who does not see that women are far more liable to the temptations of the Devil? Hence, not only when pica, uterine frenzy, or uterine epilepsy is present, etc., does he exercise his power more easily and mingle his affairs with the ordinary course of nature, but he can also entangle far more rarely men than women, and among women especially old women of inferior condition and poor upbringing, so that they serve him in the manner of witches or in whatever other way. Indeed, that temptation, the greatest and most horrible of all, which is called bodily obsession, is found more rarely in men than in women; and women who suffer from uterine frenzy or some similar affection of the womb are more liable to it still. Whatever is observed in such obsession, whether in people shut up in prison, whose neck is said to be twisted by the Devil, or in others variously torn in water, or in similar cases that bear on this, we judge can be fairly probably drawn out and proved from what has been said in these Exercitations.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CAP. IV.

units.la: (68) C A P. IV.
units.tr: (68) CHAP. IV.

units.la: De malorum Angelorum in homines Per homines Potentia.
units.tr: On the Power of Evil Angels over Men through Men.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: POffemus filum considerationis prioris ulterius extendendo ostendere multos alios modos quibus Diabolus in hominum animos illabi possit, ut illos sibi deditos & obstrictos variis modis & gradibus faciat, atque ita examinare, quomodo illi qui vanitatibus, crudelitate, crassa ignorantia, superstitione, avaritia & similibus vitiis laborant, jam ab ipso illaqueati quasi sint, & proclives redditi ut ad alia pejora transeant. Quippe haec gradus sunt, quibus ad vanas Astrologiae, Chiromantiae, Phyfiognomiae, Alchimiae & similium studiorum, quorum fundamenta nulla sunt certa, at maxime vanis praejudiciis ex infantia, sensibus, gentilismo & papatu haustis innituntur, vaniffimum cultum facile transitur. Quamvis enim astrorum vires in haec inferiora agere nullus neget; & signa quaedam in manu, facie & toto corpore possint esse, sanitatis vel morbi, quia ejus effecta sunt; & in mineralibus infinita lateant, quae inde deduci
units.tr: Pursuing the thread of our earlier consideration further, let us show the many other ways in which the Devil can slip into men's minds, so as to make them his own, bound to him in various ways and degrees. Let us also examine how those who labour under vanities, cruelty, gross ignorance, superstition, avarice and similar vices are already, as it were, ensnared by him and made prone to pass on to worse things. For these are the steps by which one passes easily to the empty worship of astrology, chiromancy, physiognomy, alchemy and similar studies. None of these has any sure foundation; they rest chiefly on vain prejudices absorbed from infancy, from the senses, from heathenism and from Papistry. It is true that no one denies that the powers of the stars act on these lower things, and that there may be certain signs in the hand, face and whole body of health or sickness, since these are their effects; and that countless things lie hidden in minerals which may be deduced from them

units.la: possunt attamen hæc adeo a tot & tam minutis circumstantiis dependent, ut non possint nisi summo labore & à Philosopho sagacissimo, & nullis non adminiculis instructo quibus rerum naturam rectâ methodo introgredi camque contemplari debet, inveniri? At plerumque hujus farinæ homines vix primorum elementorum solidæ cujusdam Philosophiæ cognitionem habent. Imo si prædicta vitia magis excellant, aut se homines profunde vanissimis studiis immerserint, quam facilis ad magiam, incantationem, præstigia; imo veneficia & similia est prolaplus?
units.tr: yet these depend on so many and such minute circumstances that they cannot be discovered except with the greatest labour, by a most sagacious philosopher, equipped with every aid, who must enter into the nature of things by the right method and contemplate it. But for the most part men of this sort hardly have any knowledge of even the first elements of solid philosophy. Indeed, if the aforesaid vices prevail more strongly, or if men have plunged themselves deeply into the most vain studies, how easy is the slide into magic, incantation and sorcery, and indeed into poisonings and similar things?

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Sed tales modos quàm plurimos quilibet, ingenii vel mediocriter subacti, excogitare poterit. At quo complementum quasi aliquod hactenus dictorum adjiciamus cum I. præter mundum & proprium corpus nostrum ad nos perdendos, Diabolus maximè etiam utatur hominibus hisce vanis tanquam suis canibus venaticis, quibus insidias primò & principaliter menti, tum corpori nectit quarum etsi graviores & notabiles magis sint illæ, quas homini obveniunt per illos qui magorum, sagarum, lamiarum, veneficarum nomine horrent, atta-men-
units.tr: Yet anyone of even moderate, trained ingenuity could devise very many such ways. But to add, as it were, a supplement to what has been said so far: besides the world and our own body, by which he ruins us, the Devil especially uses these vain men as his hunting dogs, by whom he lays snares first and principally for the mind, then for the body. Although the snares which come to a man through those whom people dread under the names of magicians, witches, hags and poisoners are more serious and more notable,

units.la: men omnes à Patre suo qui absolutè Malus dicitur, speciali jure Mali vocantur. 2 Quia horum opera non minus ac Diaboli homines admirantur & stupent, de hisce pauca adjiciemus, ex quibus patescet illos æque & multò minus ac Diabolum esse metuendis illis qui credulitatem suam iis non addicunt, & firma fide Deo suo innituntur.
units.tr: yet all of them, from their Father, who is called the Evil One absolutely, are by a special right called the Evil Ones. Since men marvel at and are astonished by the works of these people no less than by those of the Devil, we shall add a few things about them. From these it will be clear that they are to be feared equally, and much less, than the Devil by those who do not give their credulity to them and rest on their God with firm faith.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Hunc in finem tolli debet grande præjudicium, quo vulgus putat hæc opera ab ipsis Malis hominibus immediatè produci, ad instar canum qui lapidem quo petuntur mordent, neglecto illo, qui eum mittit. Ita enim illi rarissimè quid illorum patrant, sed Diabolus illorum loco; & licet illis certa corpora subministret, ut potiones, ova, poma, radices, capillos hominum, panem mendicatum, salem, herbas & similia innumera, attamen illa. Aut nihil sæpissimè agunt; quamvis decepti hoc modo sibi firmiter persuadeant se hæc illa certò patrâsse, non aliter uti pueris persuaderi solet, quòd fortem virum nutu & gestu profträrint, qui alia de causa cadit; vel simile quid fecisse quod vires eorum superat. V, gr. cum veneficæ fulmine concitato comcomburunt segetes. Cùm venatores Diabolo mancipati feras aliquas raras afferunt, quæ nunquam vilæ sunt & quas illi soli possunt capere. Novit enim Diabolus eas ex regionibus aliis adducere, si non ipsas faciat, aut, quòd potiùs judicarem, feras vulgares sub specie valde rara apparere facit, ut si v. g. cervi caput multò, magus solito oculi ignei, cornua in gyrum rotundata, cauda equinum in modum oblongata &c : exhibcatur. Sicque ipsos venatores aliosque eludit, non aliter uti per speculo & vitra arte polita facies hominis monstrosa & multiplicata ostendi poteft. Cùm sagæ in quibusdam locis infantes jam natos matribus & nutricibus subducunt & illorum loco bufones & monstrosa quædam supponunt Nam hoc etiam in continua delusione, qua sagas & omnes illos, qui potentiam talem sagis asscribunt quorumque credulitatem & animum ita prævoccupavit, consistit. Quam credulitatem ut firmet, à delusione illa statim desistit, quàm primùm virgis tales suppositītii fœtus cæduntur, sic ut prior infantium forma iterum conspici possit.
units.tr: To this end a great prejudice must be removed, by which the common people think these works are produced immediately by the Evil Ones themselves, like dogs that bite the stone with which they are struck and ignore the one who throws it. For those people very rarely accomplish anything of these things; rather the Devil does it in their place. And although he supplies them with certain substances, such as potions, eggs, apples, roots, men's hair, begged bread, salt, herbs and countless similar things, yet these things most often do nothing at all, although, deceived in this way, they firmly persuade themselves that they have certainly accomplished these deeds. It is no different from how children are usually persuaded that they have felled a strong man by a nod and gesture, when he falls for some other reason, or that they have done something similar that exceeds their powers. For example, when a witch with a thunderbolt raised up burns the crops. When hunters bound to the Devil bring in some rare wild animals, which are never seen alive and which only they can catch. For the Devil knows how to bring them from other regions, if he does not create them himself; or, which I would judge more likely, he makes ordinary wild beasts appear under a very rare form, as when, for example, the head of a stag is shown much larger than usual, with a fiery eye, horns rounded into a circle, and a tail elongated like a horse's. So he deceives the hunters and others, just as a monstrous and multiplied human face can be shown through a mirror and glass polished by art. Or when, in certain places, witches take newborn infants from their mothers and nurses and substitute toads and certain monstrous things in their place. For this also belongs to the continual delusion by which he holds the witches and all those who ascribe such power to witches, whose credulity and mind he has so thoroughly preoccupied. In order to strengthen that credulity, he immediately ceases from the delusion as soon as such substituted offspring are beaten with rods, so that the infants' former appearance can be seen again.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Atque ita judico Diabolumferè omnia illa efficere quæ omnibus illis ho-
units.tr: And so I judge that the Devil brings about nearly all those things that are attributed to all those evil men,

units.la: minibus Malis affcribuntur, quos ut altius cum credulis aliis decipiat, persuadet eis, hæc fieri per ridiculas quasdam ceremonias aut res, quas in suis artibus exercendis adhibent, uti v. gr. cantilenam, verba quædam barbara & tertiata, initium Evangelii S. Johannis, signa crucis, hostiam, nodos implicitos, congesta ossa, radicem mandragoræ, nescio quid theculæ inclusum quod spiritum familiarem vocant; & similia innumera. Nam hæc potius habenda sunt tanquam tot quasi sacramenta & signa præsentiæ Diabolicæ, sic ut dum per illas superstitiones colitur & fœdus cum ipso contractum stabilitur, statim adsit consilio & auxilio illis, qui eum colunt, ut in æternum illos perdat.
units.tr: whom, in order to deceive the credulous more deeply, he persuades that these things happen through certain ridiculous ceremonies or objects that they use in practising their arts, such as: a chant, certain barbarous words repeated three times, the opening of the Gospel of St John, signs of the cross, a host, knotted cords, gathered bones, the root of mandrake, something I know not what enclosed in a little box which they call a familiar spirit, and countless similar things. For these should rather be regarded as so many sacraments and signs of the Devil's presence, so that, while he is worshipped through these superstitions and a covenant with him is confirmed, he at once gives counsel and aid to those who worship him, in order to destroy them for eternity.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Sæpius tamen suis servis medium aliquod naturale dat, quod hæc & illa producit, attamen illi æquè sciunt quomodo hæc operentur, quàm novit rusticus quomodo agat magnes, quem jubetur ferro applicare, videtque statim ferrum versus magnetem rapi; aut si uxori suæ specificum uterinum propinat videtque illam à symptomatibus uterinis liberari. Ita enim venena diversissimarum virium aut alia quæ nanaturaliter hæc & illa mira producunt mancipiis suis tradit, quæ illi solùm applicant. Et quod miraris forsan, Diabolus per tales malos sæpe bonum quid operatur, uti medicamenta dans bona, quibus multi morbi, & præsertim illi, quos arte sua produxit, tolluntur ,quod Diabolus ab incredibili sua malitia impetrare non posse videtur. Ac ita sane est. Nil ipse commiserationis habet, sed 1. tenetur sæpius à Deo ut proprium suum opus destruat. 2. Hac simulata bonitate menti hominum insidias subtilissimas & omnium periculosissimas struit ut ab ipsa credulitatem & confidentiam impetret. Parum enim illi interest si corpori pro tempore bonum quid faciat, si mentem modò æternum (uti intentat) perdere queat, corporis enim exitium sequuturum novit. Ipsius autem multum interest, ut aliquando bonum aliquod leve producat; veritatem dicat; fidem contractus servet, amicum & angelum bonum &c: simulet, ut eo ipso regnum suum magis stabiliat. Nunquam enim magis quàm sub specie veri & boni nocet, nec unquam plus metuendus est; unde vulgus dicere solet, quòd si Diabolus tam niger appareret, uti est, nullum ad se trahiturum.
units.tr: Yet he often gives his servants some natural means that produces this or that, though they know just as little how these things work as a country man knows how a magnet acts when he is told to bring it near iron, and sees the iron at once drawn toward the magnet; or as when he gives his wife a specific remedy for the womb and sees her freed from womb ailments. For so he hands over to his malos servants poisons of the most diverse powers, or other things that naturally produce this or that marvel, which they merely apply. And what you perhaps wonder at: the Devil through such malos often does some good, as when he gives good medicines by which many diseases, and especially those which he himself has produced by his art, are cured. This the Devil, from his incredible malice, seems unable to obtain. And indeed so it is. He has no compassion whatever, but 1. he is often compelled by God to destroy his own work; 2. by this feigned goodness he lays the most subtle snares for men's minds, and the most dangerous of all, so as to win their credulity and confidence. For it matters little to him if for the moment he does some good to the body, provided he can destroy the soul for eternity (as he threatens), since he knows that the ruin of the body will follow. It is greatly in his interest, however, that he now and then produce some slight good, tell the truth, keep faith in a bargain, and feign friendship and a good angel, etc., so that by this very means he may establish his kingdom more firmly. For he never harms more than under the appearance of truth and good, and never is he more to be feared; whence the common people are wont to say that if the Devil appeared as black as he is, he would draw no one to himself.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Ut autem ulterius præjudicia nostra deponamus,notari hîc bene potest,quòd, quia Diabolus integram rerum naturam intimè perspectam habet, possit cuidam suorum mancipiorum quædam stupenda Naturæ arcana detegere, etsi non addat causas per quas hæc & illa fiant.
